Uniform Title: *Candrajñānāgama* Manuscript: IFP/EFEO Transcript T0012 Description: The *Candrajñāna* is a Siddhānta upāgama that defines [its subject matter].
It is itself a *pratiṣṭhātantra*, that is, a tantra dealing with the ritual procedures for the installation and worship of representations of Śaiva deities, including *liṅgas*.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: April 8, 2012.
Country of publication: India.
Hari Om!
The Candrajñāna, the five-syllabled, supreme secret, whose nature is the form of ultimate bliss.
This shall be the supreme secret; listen, you who are dear to my welfare.
Through the dual contemplation of the gross and the subtle, one contemplates that which is subtler than the subtle—the blissful Praṇava, the seed-syllable, whose form is blissful dance. || 2 ||
Dhyāna is declared to be Naṭeśvara, the Śiva who is supreme among the five-syllabled [mantra];
the five-syllabled [mantra] is the Supreme Brahman, pure and the destroyer of impurities. (3)
The letter Ya is the face of Īśāna, while the letter Va is the face of Tatpuruṣa; the letter Śi is the face of Aghora... [and so forth].
And the letter *ya* is Sadāśiva, whose presiding deities are the five [faces]. (5)
Listen to the procedure for the five-syllable mantra, which is the gross, subtle, and supreme light:
the syllable *na*, the syllable *ma*, the syllable *śi*, and the syllable *va*. (6)
The six-syllabled mantra beginning with the *praṇava* has the letter *ya* joined with five others;
among these syllables, the *praṇava* is primary, and the syllable is preceded by knowledge.
The Praṇava is declared to be the imperishable syllable, the abode of all mantras;
a mantra devoid of the Praṇava would be as if deprived of life.
Among all mantras, the *praṇava* is said to be the life-force (*prāṇa*) of mantras;
it is joined with the first vowel and joined with the fifth vowel. (9)
Joined with the end of the sixth group [of consonants] and endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*, that is declared to be the *praṇava*, auspicious and the bestower of all accomplishments. (10)
The syllable *dhānta* (dha), joined with the third vowel (*u*), and *bhanta* (bha) likewise joined with the third vowel;
then *mānta* (ma) endowed with a long vowel and the letter *lānta* (la)—this is the supreme five-syllabled mantra. (11)
The three syllables are the letter *oṃ*, the letter *na*, and the letter *ma*.
The letter *va* is masculine, while the letter *śi* is joined with the feminine. (12)
The letter *ya* should be known as the neuter; thus, from there, the three follow in sequence:
the letter *na* is the Ṛgveda, and the letter *ma* is the Yajurveda. (13)
The letter Śa would be the Sāmaveda; the letter Ma would be the Atharva-veda;
and the letter Ya would be the Itihāsa, which likewise consists of all the gods. (14)
The color, the deity, as well as the power (śakti), the support (ādhāra), and the meter (chandas);
the sage (ṛṣi), the station (sthāna), the Brahman, and likewise the weapon—these are [to be known]. || 15 ||
The quality of art (kalāguṇa), the wheel (cakra), illumination (prakāśa),
the instrument (karaṇa), the wind (vāyu), and the organ of knowledge (jñānendriya)— these are the sixteen in sequence.
The letter *na* is the form of the earth, and Brahmā is the presiding deity therein;
Sāvitrī is said to be its power (*śakti*), and the earth is likewise its support (*ādhāra*).
It is joined with the Anuṣṭubh meter, and Vasiṣṭha is its seer;
its location is in the western face, which is Sadyojāta, the first Brahman.
The weapon is said to be the thunderbolt alone, and the digit is indeed Nivṛtti.
On the marking of the qualities, Menā is [assigned] by means of the cloud; thus the fourfold wheel has been declared. (19)

The instrument of action, as well as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), together with the vital breath (prāṇavāyu), the sense organ, and indeed the olfactory faculty (gandhaka)— all these are illuminated by the light of the kindled fire.
Thus, among these sixteen, the syllable *na* is declared;
this syllable *na* has been explained—now hear the syllable *ma*.
The letter *ma* is indeed the form of water, as well as the deity Viṣṇu;
it is conjoined with the power Lakṣmī and is the support, which is water itself.
It is joined with the Triṣṭubh meter, and Viśvāmitra is the seer;
the northern face is Vāmadeva, which belongs to Brahmā. (23)
And indeed Padmāyudha, as well as Pratiṣṭhā and Kalā;
there may also be Guṇadravya, and likewise Cakra and Ardhenduja. (24)
The instrument is indeed the intellect, illuminated by the light of the moon and the sun;
and in the downward breath (apāna), the form of wind becomes the faculty of taste, which is a sense organ of knowledge.
Thus, among these sixteen, the letter *ma* is proclaimed;
now hear the letter *śi*.
The syllable ŚI is the form of fire, and Rudra is the presiding deity there;
it is conjoined with the power Gaurī, and Agni himself is the support.
Joined with the Triṣṭubh meter, Jamadagni likewise [is situated there];
the Aghora face and Brahmā are located in the southern position.
The weapon is said to be the svastika, while the fire of knowledge is indeed the kalā;
it is endowed with the radiance of the qualities (guṇas), and the wheel is indeed three-pointed. (29)
The instrument, the mind, is like lightning in its radiance;
likewise, the organ of knowledge is manifest as form.
Thus, among these sixteen, the syllable *śi* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
This syllable *śi* has been proclaimed; now listen to the syllable *va*.
The letter *va* is the form of Vāyu; its presiding deity is Īśvara.
Ambikā is the Great Śakti, and Vāyu is indeed her support. (32)
Connected with the Bṛhatī meter, the seer is said to be Kāśyapa;
its position is in the eastern face, and that is Brahmā. || 33 ||
The support is in the form of the drop (bindu), as well as the digit (kalā) and tranquility (śānti);
it is not joined with the touch of the qualities (guṇa-sparśa), and it is indeed the six-pointed wheel. (34)
The lamp-light is said to be the instrument, as is the mind itself;
thus, these are declared to be the [components] of the sixteen vowels. This syllable "va" has been explained; now listen to the syllable "ya."
The form of the letter Ya is indeed the divine Sadāśiva;
joined with the power Unmanī, it is called the support, the void (vyoma). || 37 ||
One should know that it is joined with the Jagatī meter, has Bharadvāja as its seer (ṛṣi), and its location is facing upwards; it is Brahmā and Īśāna himself.
Among weapons, it is the trident; it is indeed the digit beyond tranquility (śāntyātīta-kalā).
Its quality is emptiness, which is the radiance of the moonstone. (39)

The instrument (karaṇa) consists of the form of primordial nature (prakṛti), as well as the equalized vital air (samānavāyu), and the organ of hearing; these are the sixteen [evolutes] in their proper order. (40)
This syllable *ya* has been declared as neither having existed nor being about to exist; this has been declared as the five-syllabled [mantra]. Now, listen to the syllable of the *praṇava*.
The Praṇava is indeed the form of the self, with the Supreme Self as its presiding deity;
the goddess Svāhā is the Great Power (Mahāśakti), the support, the supreme state. || 42 ||
The supreme station of the sages, joined with the Gāyatrī metre, is declared to be the mouth of Śiva; O Brahmā, that mouth of Śiva shall become [the source]. 43.
The weapon is said to be indeed empty, and its digit (kalā) is also empty;
the wheel is without qualities, free from affliction, luminous, and consisting of a hundred thousand [spokes]. (44)
"Niṣkara" means that there is no wind [of agitation] among the sixteen sense organs;
thus, for these sixteen, [the mantra is] "Oṃ," and for the Oṃ, "Salutation. (45)
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* which is the *bindu*;
the half-moon, the *nirodhin*, the *nāda*, and the end of *nāda*. || 46 ||
Śakti, Vyāpinī, Samānā, and likewise Unmanā;
the net of bonds extends up to the end of Samānā—thus do they consider Paraśiva. (47)
The seven-crore great mantra is the cause of mental agitation;
the single-syllable great mantra transcends the fourth state and brings about the dissolution of the mind.
He who does not find the Praṇava endowed with sixteen parts (dviraṣṭaka-kala) is neither a mantra-practitioner nor a teacher; he merely undergoes fruitless hardship in ritual acts. (49)

The utterance of the *bīja* is the waking state; dreaming consists of the grasping of the *bindu*; deep sleep is the conjunction with the *nāda*; and the fourth state (*turya*) is attained through union with the *śakti*.
The state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) is taught as the peaceful dissolution in the supreme light;
having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
The syllable *na* is the form of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the syllable *ma* is the form of maintenance (*sthiti*),
the syllable *śi* is withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), and the syllable *va* is concealment (*tirobhava*).
The syllable *ya* is grace (*anugraha*), and this world consists of five syllables;
the syllable *na* is joined with the Kṛta age, while the syllable *ma* becomes the Tretā Yuga. (53)
The letter Śa is the Kṛta age, Ya is the Dvāpara, and likewise Ra is the Kali age; Ya is the interval between ages (Yugāntara). This world consists of these five syllables. (54)
The Śaiva, the Pāśupata, the Buddhist, the Ārhata, the Kāpāla, and the Pāñcarātra—these six are known as the traditional systems (samayas). || 55 ||

The student (brahmacārī) should perform the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa); for the householder, it is the placement of maintenance (sthitinyāsa); but for forest-dwellers and ascetics, the placement of withdrawal (saṃhāranyāsa) is prescribed.
One should place the syllable *ya* with the thumb, the syllable *va* on the index finger;
the syllable *śi* with the middle finger, and the syllable *ma* on the ring finger. (57)
The letter *na* should be placed on the little finger; this is declared to be the *sṛṣṭinyāsa*.
Having placed the letter *ya* on the head, one should place the letter *va* on the forehead. (58)
Having placed the syllable ŚI at the heart, the syllable MA at the region of the navel,
and the syllable NA at the feet, one should place the Praṇava (Om) upon all the limbs.
The syllable *na* is for the purification of the self; the syllable *ma* is the purification of the locus;
the syllable *śi* is the purification of the sign (*liṅga*); such is the sequence of the ritual involving the five purifications. (60)
The earth is to be known as infinite, and likewise water is the lion-throne;
this is declared to be the yoga of fire, and similarly the form of wind.
The sky is indeed stainless, as is the sequence of the ritual for the five seats;
invocation is performed with the letter *na*, while installation is performed with the letter *ma*.
One should worship Śiva, the supreme cause, with the syllable *śi* for his presence, with the syllable *vā* for the offering of water (*arghya*), and with the syllable *ya*. (64)
The wise practitioner should conceive of the seat (pīṭha) as having the form of the Praṇava;
it consists of the five kalās of the letter *na* and the four kalās of the letter *ma*. (65)
One should assign eight digits to the syllable Śi, thirteen to the syllable Va, and eight digits to the syllable Ya;
thus one should place the digits of the five-syllabled mantra.
The letter Śa is indeed the form of Śiva, while the letter Va is Śakti herself;
the letter Ya is the form of the Self (Ātman), and the letter Na is concealment (Tirobhava).
The syllable *ma* is indeed the form of impurity; thus the five-syllabled [mantra] is remembered. The syllable *na* is the invocation, and the syllable *ma* is the lotus seal (*padmamudrikā*). (68)
One should employ the letter Śa as the fist-mudrā, the letter Va as the yoga-mudrā, the letter Ya as the liṅga-mudrā, and [the letter Ra] as the śiva-mudrā. || 69 ||
The letter *ya* is joined with the *liṅga*, the letter *va* is the stalk itself,
the letter *śi* is the upper lotus, and the letter *ma* is the throat itself. (70)
The letter *na* at the lower lotus is called the *liṅga*;
through its worship one gains a vast kingdom, and through the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), one attains prosperity.
Through recitation (japa), there is purification from sin; through meditation (dhyāna), there is bliss and liberation.
The syllable *na* removes sin, and the syllable *ma* grants release from sin.
(16) There is no god equal to Mahādeva anywhere in the three worlds;
there is no mantra equal to the five-syllabled one, O Great Sage. (73)
"The five-syllabled great mantra, the sacred ash as the supreme medicine, and Mahādeva as the highest kinsman—this is the certain conclusion of the scripture. (74)
In the Āgama it is said:
"In the middle is Śiva, then Śakti, and then the Self, which is forgotten. That which precedes it is declared to be the binder; that which precedes even that is the remover of bondage. (75)
Elsewhere it is said: "The letter Śa is the form of Śiva; the letter Va is called Śakti;
the letter Ya is conjoined with the Self (Ātman); and the letter Na is concealment (tirobhava). (76)
The letter *ma* is of the nature of impurity (*mala*); it is remembered as the "five-syllabled" (*pañcākṣara*).
As stated in the *Devikālottara*:
Obstruction is said to be water; it is the power of the Self, whose essence is Śiva. || 77 ||
"O Goddess, one should not reveal this five-syllabled secret;
it is the fierce five-syllabled mantra. O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Omniscient One, Abode of Compassion! (78)
I truly desire to hear the secret of the five syllables in their essential reality—the supreme five-syllable mantra, the secret that bestows liberation. (79)
For the sake of attaining desires, this should be concealed with great effort along with its ritual materials;
it must never be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple. (80)
The seven-crore great mantra is the cause of mental agitation;
this five-syllabled [mantra], O Goddess, is renowned throughout the three worlds. (81)
One should mutter this five-syllabled mantra, which is meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin;
by the mere recollection of which, even the killing of a Brahmin is removed. (82)
Thus, O Goddess, listen to that great mantra of five syllables;
hereafter, I shall explain the sequence of the ritual procedure for the five syllables.
Oṃ!
Having offered salutations to Śiva, I shall explain the fivefold name [of the mantra], consisting of the syllable *na*, the syllable *ma*, and likewise the syllable *śi*. (84)
They know the letter *va* and the letter *ya* to be this five-syllabled [mantra].
O Goddess, this five-syllabled [mantra] is proclaimed to be the five deities. || 85 ||
The five-syllable mantra is pure and consists of the five Brahmans;
likewise, it is composed of earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The Great God Pañcabrahma is established within the five principles (pañcatattva):
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 87 ||
The syllable *na* is the form of Brahmā; the syllable *ma* is the form of Viṣṇu;
the syllable *śi* is the form of Rudra; and likewise, the syllable *va* is Īśvara.
The letter *ya* is to be known as Sadāśiva; these are the presiding deities.
The letter *na* is golden-colored, while the letter *ma* is black-colored. (89)
The letter Śa is the color of fire, the letter Va is dark blue, and the letter Ya has the appearance of crystal; thus the distinctions of their colors are proclaimed. (90)
The syllable *na* is Sadyojāta, while *ma* is Vāmadeva;
*śi* is joined with Aghora, and *va* is known as Tatpuruṣa.
The letter *ya* is declared to be the sky (*gagana*); the various types of faces have been proclaimed.
The letter *na* shall be the *Ṛgveda*, while the letter *ma* is the *Yajurveda*. (92)
The letter ŚA is the Sāmaveda, the letter VA is the Atharvaveda, and the letter YA is the Itihāsa, the majesty of the beginning of all the Vedas. (93)
Therefore, the five-syllable mantra should always belong to the speaker;
it is the god whose supreme state is the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise the syllable *oṃ* which is supreme. (94)
This six-syllable mantra begins with the syllable *oṃ* and ends with the syllable *ya*.
The syllable *na* is to be known as pertaining to pacification (*śāntika*), and likewise, the syllable *ma* is for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). (95)
The syllable ŚI is for malevolent rites (abhicāra), the syllable VA is for subjugation (vaśya), and the syllable YA is indeed the bestower of liberation; these follow the sequence of the single form.
(21) As long as there is success or even when there is no success, one should always perform recitation in that manner;
he who offers recitation at every step, O Goddess, is truly wise. || 97 ||
This supreme five-syllabled [mantra] shall bring about all accomplishments;
thus should this five-syllabled mantra, difficult to obtain even in the three worlds, be known. (98)
Thus ends the chapter on the Five Syllables in the Vidyāpurāṇa:
The syllable *U* is said to be the goddess Umā, and the syllable *A* is said to be Śiva;
the union of these two is known as the Pīṭha and the Liṅga. (1)
In the *Cidambararahasya*:

"The letter *na* as the feet, the letter *ma* as the belly, the letter *śi* as the mouth, the letter *kā* as the wind, and the letter *ra* as the head—those who meditate upon this divine form of five syllables in this sequence attain liberation while living. (2)
The syllable Śi is said to be the crown; the syllable Va is called the arm;
the syllable Ya is the hand of fearlessness; and the syllable Na is the form of fire. (3)
The letter *ma* is the lotus of the feet; Śiva, who is ever present as Apasmāra, stands above that and performs the dance of bliss.
The Praṇava is the eternal abode of Śrī for the Lord of Tāṇḍava;
in the blissful Tāṇḍava dance, Śiva performs his own creative act.
Creation resides in the ḍamaruka; maintenance resides in the hand holding the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya);
dissolution resides in the form of fire; and concealment resides in the firm foot.
And Śiva bestows grace upon those whose feet are turned away from Him;
having shaken off illusion and burnt away sin, which destroys knowledge, He grants liberation.
Having performed [the ritual] and extracted [the essence], with the hand of Śiva-knowledge, he established the Supreme Self within the ocean of bliss as the eternal Śiva-tāṇḍava dance. (8)
The five-syllabled [mantra] is in the midst of the supreme; the dancer consists of the five syllables.
The great forest is seventy million [in extent], as are the moving and non-moving beings.
That great liṅga of seventy million is Śiva, the abode of the Tāṇḍava dance;
within that abode of Tāṇḍava, however, resides the partless (niṣkala) form, which is difficult for others to attain.
This is another secret, which is as if unutterable and not to be revealed; yet reveal this knowledge of mine to my devotees, O lady with the beautiful face.
It should be protected with great effort, just as wealth is guarded from thieves;
it is filled by means of the five-syllable mantra, beginning from the big toe and ending at the little toe.
The heel is indeed [indicated] by the letter *na*, while the ankle is represented by *ma*;
the knee and thigh are *śi*, and the region of the genitals is *va*. (13)
The syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) is the foundation, and in its center is the letter *na*;
the letter *ya* is said to be the waist, and the letter *ra* is the region of the back. (14)
The syllable ŚI is said to be the navel; the syllable MA is located in the region of the belly;
the syllable VA is the place of the heart; and the syllable YA is located in the region of the breasts. || 15 ||
The syllable *na* is located in the chest, the syllable *śi* in the region of the arms,
the syllable *ma* is said to be in the elbow, and the syllable *va* at the wrist.
The syllable *ya* is mounted upon the base [of the thumb], starting from the thumb and proceeding in sequence;
the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) is the syllable *ma*, and the bracelet shall be the *praṇava*.

The letter *ta* is said to be "thread" (*tantra*), the letter *śi* is declared to be "skin" (*carma*); they say the letter *va* is "the shore" (*taṭi*), and the sound is the mantra named "Name" (*nāda*). (18)
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, listen to [the description of] the hand of protection (abhayahasta):
in that hand there is a serpent, which is the subtle five-syllabled mantra. 19.
O Maheśvara, my light exists in the form of fire in my left hand;
likewise, by my other hand, you are the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction.
The syllable *na* is said to be the neck; the syllable *ma* is the region of the throat;
the syllable *śi* is the region of the jaw; and the syllable *va* is the region of the mouth. || 21 ||
The letter *ya* is the region of the nose; next, hear about the three eyes:
the letter *na* is the eye of all, and the letter *ma* is the left eye.
The syllable *śi* is the upward eye, while the syllable *va* is with the ear;
one should place the *praṇava* between the eyebrows and the brilliantly radiant *haṃsa* in the center. (23)
Having placed the letter *ya* on the head as well as on the limbs and sub-limbs, the twelve-syllable mantra is thus declared to be the "Jaṭācūḍa. (24)
The seed-syllable of Māyā, water, and likewise Dhūr-dharā and the rest,
combined with all the letters, is known as Indukhaṇḍa.
The body is indeed composed of five syllables, while the embodied soul is known through the name-mantra;
it is the stainless Śiva, partless, dancing the dance of bliss.
One should learn this five-syllable yantra from the mouth of the guru;
it must not be given to one who is not a son, nor likewise to one who is not a disciple. (27)
(27) This assembly mechanism has been declared for one’s own son, or for one who is like a son, who is righteous and steadfast. Now hear the worship involving the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (28)
The *Nṛttapañcākṣara* is completed.
Śrī Candra said:
O God of gods, O Great Lord, O ornament of the lords of gods and nāgas!
The ritual bathing has been fully described; now tell me of the festival, O Śaṅkara.
Īśvara said:
Now, O Lord of Kalās, I shall describe the supreme festival arising from conjunction;
know that the festival is of seven kinds—listen with a one-pointed mind. (2)
The Śākta, Cārva, Brāhma, Maukta, Śāmbhava, Āṇava,
and that which is renowned as Arkaja— O Moon, these are the nine faces.
(28) It is said that the Śākta [observance] lasts for nine days, the Ārṣaka for seven days;
the Brāhmaka is declared to last five days, and the Maunika is said to last three days. || 4 ||

One should know that a single day brings peace; it may be for a Brāhmaṇa or a wandering ascetic. On a Sunday coinciding with the Arka-janman (the Sun's birthday), there shall be sevenfold festivities here.
One should raise the banner in due order in the Śākta and Brāhma [mandalas];
in the sixth, one should raise the banner with the mantra "ma" which is dark blue and possesses the splendor of the sun.
That day is threefold; and two [days] are twofold in the first [category], while there is none in the last.
One should first raise the banner: the superior, the middling, and the inferior.
I shall speak correctly regarding the day of the sacred ford (tīrtha); listen well, O you who are marked by the arrow!
[The asterisms] Citrā, Viśākhā, Mūla, and Uttarāṣāḍhā as well— || 8 ||
Śraviṣṭhā, Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Maghā, and the Uttarā constellation [are assigned] to the twelve signs beginning with Aries. (9)
In all months, the festival should be performed ending with the constellation Ārdrā;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha it should end on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and in Māgha it should end on the sixth day.
On the new moon day, on the full moon day, or on any other auspicious day,
or at the birth or death of kings, or during battle, or at the birth of the patron (yajamāna).

On the day of the consecration, a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) should be prepared, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is excellent for the sake of dharma, grants desires, and indeed arises from ritual action throughout the entire month.
Alternatively, it is said that the moon grants creation;
therefore, the festival for the one marked by the hare (the moon) should be performed in whichever month [it occurs]. (13)
In that month, everything should be performed according to the prescribed rules;
from the raising of the flag and the consecration of the sprouts up to the final ritual at the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), it is traditionally taught that this month is supreme for such rites.
From the raising of the banner (dhvaja) up to the pilgrimage site (tīrtha), that month is indeed the middle one;
in the preceding month, the raising of the banner took place, as well as the festival held therein. || 15 ||
We shall now describe another procedure known as Adhaman;
having first established the sacrifice in that month at an excellent sacred site.
Because of their absence, that which has been performed is considered to grant supreme happiness;
however, the mixing of festivals for deities residing in a single sacred site is [not so]. || 17 ||
I shall tell you that which leads to the agitation of the kingdom when it is devoid of those [qualities];
O Moon, whatever site is constructed shall likewise be of two kinds. (18)
The miscellaneous minor [rites] have been explained; now hear concerning the festive and transformative [rites].
First, [one should perform them] from the boundary of the foot-protectors all around, or in a single location. (19)
That which is outside the enclosure wall of a dwelling is called *prakīrṇaka*;
that which extends to the edge of the enclosure wall is *brāhmya*, while that which is situated within it is designated as *kṣudravāstuka*.
Its boundary is the Brahma-pada; the Aindra and other [directions] are the Śāntaka-pada.
From this, from that, and from this one, it is the Vāstuka-pada.
In that very place, one who desires all accomplishments should perform the worship of the gods, the offering of oblations, and circumambulation. (22)
Furthermore, in this abode, he who performs the festival of Śiva in a place other than the royal capital would be superior to one who gives gifts at other sacred fords (tīrthas). || 23 ||
Even at a sacred ford (tīrtha), when it is not the time for a festival, one should perform the Śaiva festival together with fellow practitioners.
[One should wear] a fine, very smooth, and beautiful new cloth, like a thread from a subtle shuttle.
Having divided the length into five parts, the width shall be one part;
it should first be equal to the height, and above that, there shall be the spire (śikhara).
It should be provided with two tails and three humps, and at its peak it should be adorned with small bells;
in its center, one should mark a bull using white, red, and other colors.
Then, having arranged either a standing posture or a reclining posture upon the lotus seat,
one should sequentially draw the parasol, the two chowries, and the water-pot.
The characteristics of the banner have been declared; now hear in due order concerning the banner-pole:
sandalwood, campaka, sāla, jackfruit, and devadāru wood. (28)
The seat may be made of *vakula*, *madhyaka*, or even [other woods],
as well as *bilva*, *punnāga*, *khadira*, *kramuka*, and coconut. (29)
Thus it has been declared: the supreme [height] is three times the width of the temple (prāsāda), or twice as much, or equal, or less by one-quarter, or even half.
Whether ending at the bull (the base) or at the gate-tower (gopura), according to what has been stated and declared;
having then set aside half of the door-panel (kavāṭa), the remainder is called the height (utsedha).
It is not said to be five *tālas*, four *tālas*, or three *tālas*;
rather, it is made firm by two parts out of five parts of the height of the staff.
The palm [measurement] joined with the plastering is not indeed for the Vaiṣṇava [temple];
rather, one should take a staff half of that, in the middle of the three-palm measurement.
One should attach a suitable iron ring to the tip of the staff;
furthermore, one should cause three additional staffs to be provided at the front, each exceeding [the previous] by three *tālas*.
One should firmly and auspiciously bind it with the tip of the staff at its base, middle, and top;
having made a cord from a fine thread, its thickness should be equal to that of the middle finger.
One should attach a ring that is twice as long as the staff;
at the tip of the staff, it should be joined with a brush and encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass. (36)
One should install the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) either between the pedestal and the gateway, or in front of the bull,
prior to the day of the flag-raising ceremony.
One should dig a pit measuring twelve, five, or four tālas in depth;
it should contain a gold niṣka, or three-quarters, or half, or even half of a quarter of a niṣka of gold.
One should cast either a tortoise, or a bull, or a golden lotus into the *vaṭa* tree;
with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should establish it firmly and immovably. (39)
The wise one should fashion the pedestal with thirty-one finger-breadths;
its height should be equal to its width, or even less by one-quarter.
One should fashion a lotus above, joined with a *karṇikā* and a *tāla*, provided with either three or two girdles (*mekhalā*), or else with a single girdle. (41)
One should consecrate the banner on the night preceding the day of its hoisting;
or else, the consecration should be performed on that very day during the morning hours.
In front of the palace, in a beautiful pavilion well-adorned, bright and smeared with cow dung, and sprinkled with auspicious water; || 43 ||
p.
36) A wise person should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there in six locations;
the intelligent one should fashion a lotus and arrange the seat in due order. (44)
One should prepare a sacrificial seat with *darbha* grass and worship each [deity] slowly;
having respectfully installed Candraśekhara upon the western altar, one should proceed. (45)
One should worship the Annaliṅga at its front, and a trident (śūla) in front of that;
then a bull and a water-pot (vṛṣakumbha) in front of that, and likewise a banner (dhvaja) in front of that.
Having established the drum to its east, one should worship it in due order;
each should be worshipped with a new cloth and with [offerings such as] incense and so forth.
Then one should cast the oblation and cause betel-leaf to be offered;
one should perform the ritual sprinkling of the eyes, especially for the bull that bears the banner.
One should tie a protective amulet (kautuka) there on the right horn; having wrapped it with a fine thread, it should be filled with two āḍhakas [of grain]. (49)
[He should place] gold richly adorned with garments filled with perfumes;
[and] on all sides, eight jars presided over by the world-protectors (lokapāla) as their deities. || 50 ||
Each [vessel] should be joined with a ritual brush (kūrca) and individually wrapped in cloth; having completed the rite with its own root mantra, one should then prepare that fire.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila); otherwise, having first performed the preliminary rites, they [the disciples] should be consecrated by the five purificatory ceremonies (pañcasaṃskāra).
One should offer one hundred oblations with wood from the roots of the *uddhāna* and other trees, along with *samit* fuel, mustard seeds, and the roots and parts of the *vṛṣa* plant. (53)
With the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra, using the syllable *pṛṣṭha* and *sudarbhayā*, one should offer oblations with the five Brahma-mantras; thus one shall accomplish the full [rite]. || 54 ||
One should especially worship the primary liṅgas and other [images] with [the appropriate] substances;
this should be performed at night, and [the remaining rites] in the morning.
Having performed the circumambulation of the temple while adorned with all ornaments,
the preceptors should, if the raising of the banner has been preceded by this, perform it with the banner itself during the day.
Having performed circumambulations with silver, one should move about at night;
one should raise the banner by means of the Yantra, using the mantra of the Vṛṣagāyatrī.
Having first bound the *rohaṇa*, one should subsequently cause it to grow by means of sequential application;
then, with the consecrated jars, one should properly install [it] in the mandala.
One should offer mung-bean rice, milk-rice, beef, pure rice, and kṛsara;
then, having performed the food-offering at night, one should commence the worship of the Liṅga. (59)
One should worship the deities in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, ending with the sacrificial oblation;
thereafter, one should worship the drum, and after that, the preceptor.
With garments, ornaments, perfumes, and the like, with flower garlands and decorations,
the preceptor should strike the drum three times with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should beat [the drum] for all the worlds to become manifest;
thereafter, one should worship the musical instruments, cymbals, and time-keeping devices.
One should especially offer an oblation (bali) accompanied by a bull and its herd;
one should perform the circumambulation of the village together with the deities of the weapons and others.
Having summoned Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as the thirty-three deities, he should worship them and offer a bali-oblation with their respective mantras. (64)
The preceptor is the sacred ford and the lamps; indeed, the preceptor with a satisfied mind—this has been declared by you, O embodiment of truth, prior to the hoisting of the banner. (65)
One should strike the drum at night and, having performed a circumambulation by means of the banner itself,
one should raise the flagstaff preceded by the striking of the drum.
On festival days and other such occasions, the preeminent Ādiśaiva guru,
having first performed the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), should then strike the drum.
Thereafter, one should raise the banner following the ritual of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa);
if done in the forenoon, O twice-born, there will be prosperity, while at night it increases the wealth of Śūdras.
But if the raising of the banner occurs at night, O Moon,
one should always worship it with special care, as well as the trident-banner. (69)
One should first have the chariots, the festive processional elements, and their constituent parts made in due order;
likewise, the palanquins and all kinds of specialized mechanical devices.
Many carts, vehicles, carriages, elephants, horses, and the like; as well as various types of umbrellas, peacock-feather fans, chowries, and fly-whisks. || 71 ||
Banners, canopies, and various kinds of flags; garments and ornaments, as well as all types of excellent vessels. || 72 ||
Everything is possible for one of great resolve; one should act according to one's capacity.
One should decorate the temple in due order, from the base (upāna) up to the pinnacle (sthūpi).

One should construct walls, pavilions, gate-towers (gopura), and so forth within the pavilion; and according to one's desire or specific instruction, one should prepare the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇṭapa) for the circumambulation.
Then, having constructed a pavilion all around the temple and even beyond it,
as well as auspicious water-stalls (prapās) adorned with canopies and banners.
Her limbs were covered with various garments, pearl necklaces, flower garlands, silk ribbons, divine ornaments, bells, chowries, and sprouts. || 76 ||
Having specifically fashioned it with hanging fruits and flowers of coconut and betel-nut trees, and adorned with all types of ornaments; || 77 ||
One should properly adorn the doors with incense, lamps, and flowers,
as well as with arches, banners, cloths, plantains, and areca nuts.
Having thus adorned the doors with sprouts, the roots of *darbha* grass, full water-jars, and young shoots, as well as the village temple, [he should proceed]. (79)
Having adorned the village streets and lanes according to the previously established rites for success,
and having made the ground level by removing depressions and elevations, one should purify it by sprinkling water.
Having smeared it with powdered flour and especially having painted it,
it should be beautified with banners and flags that reach toward the sky.
It was adorned with plantains, betel-nut trees, door-pitchers, lamps, and incense burners;
it was canopied with perfumes, garlands, sprouts, umbrellas, jars, and cloths.
Having prepared for the meditation, one should have a sacrificial pavilion constructed,
provided with sixteen pillars, either in the northeast or in the southeast.
The middle section is excellent with nine, seven, and five cubits;
it is provided with gates, archways, and banners, and adorned with canopies and flags. (84)
On the pillar, it should be joined with a winding [decoration] made of darbha grass garlands, sprouts, and so forth;
within the sacrificial altar (antarvedi), there should be eighty-one squares formed by nine squares each.
One should especially construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) there according to the previously mentioned procedure, having a height of one cubit (ratna) and resembling the surface of a mirror.
Having made it level everywhere and smeared it with cow-dung water,
one should adorn it with the five powders and beautify it with sprouts and other ornaments.

Having thus prepared the sacrificial hall with incense, lamps, unbroken grains, and flowers, and provided it with a concealed canopy, one should construct a pavilion for the purpose of the forest procession.
One should construct it at a desired location, either somewhat distant or nearby,
and surrounded by hidden *campaka*, *aśoka*, *sāla*, *campaka*, and *bilva* trees. (89)
With *lavaṅga*, *karṇikāra*, silver, iron, and *dhāmamayu* trees; with *panasa*, coconut palms, plantains, betel nuts, and mangoes. (90)
With *punnāga* and *kurava* trees,
with *pāṭala* trees, and also with *ketakī*, *mātuluṅga*, *likuca*, and *pippala* trees.
With leaves and flowers of the udumbara, vaṭa, and plakṣa trees, and with the three-leafed [plant], nimba, dāru, and kapittha; || 92 ||
One should construct a pavilion in the center for those beginning with the aforementioned [deities], adorned with flowers and water, and on its sides, a place for water-sports.
Outside, it is enclosed by a wall and adorned with gates and gate-towers.
Having done this, [he should worship him] especially endowed with all ornaments;
likewise, he should perform all the other many components of the festival in a special manner. (95)
Having remained mindful, the festival should be performed by the people as previously described;
specifically on the night of the tenth day, following the auspicious lunar date of the sacred ford (tīrtha).
O God, one should establish the sacrifice;
it is ordained for Nāvaha on days consisting of the elements (5), arrows (5), qualities (3), and one (1), [or] on days [numbered] by the eyes (2) and so forth. || 97 ||
Having established the sacrificial offerings before him during the nights,
the preceptor, the leader of the stars, [should place them] upon the altar in the center of the sacrificial pavilion.
(On page 47:
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center, divided into five parts;
with eight droṇas of śāli rice, and above that, with half as much unhusked grain.
One should tie it with half a thread;
having uttered the heart-mantra, one should tie it upon the middle petal. || 100 ||

One should spread darbha grass upon the sacrificial mound and prepare jars filled with a drona-measure of water; having marked them with a thread, one should arrange three jars adorned with various threads.
Then, having prepared a seat in the southern half of the pericarp,
one should place [the deity] there, and also the *vardhanī* vessel starting from its left side with the root mantras.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should place nine gems;
however, if gems are unavailable, one should place a golden lotus in the *vardhanī* vessel and a golden utpala flower.
Having joined it with the ritual *kūrca* grass and wrapped it in a new cloth,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and then cause the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) to be offered with the root mantra. || 104 ||
One should place jars containing the eight Vidyeśvaras around the eight petals;
having filled them all with scented water, one should worship them with their respective mantras.
Into those [vessels], one should place weapons made of gold, beginning with the vajra and ending with the trident;
having covered each individually with cloths, they should be provided with tufts of grass and circular bases.
Some may arrange nine, seven, five, three, or one fire-pit according to their means or according to their desire. || 107 ||
In the cardinal and intermediate directions, with nine at the front, the singing should then take place in the east;
likewise in the south from the east, in the north, and in the region of the northeast.
One should arrange the seven fires between the Īśāna and Cakra fires;
one should also arrange the five fires with offerings in the four directions. || 109 ||
Indra is in the southern triad and in front of the single fire-altar;
one should perform the rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires according to the previously stated procedure.
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, rice, śāli rice, barley, wheat, and viṣṇu-grain; wild rice, jāla-rice, saṃtā-rice, as well as black gram, green gram, and kulattha—these are [the offerings]. (111)
One should offer a *rājamāṣa* and an *āḍhaka* measure of sesame seeds that are free from impurities and fresh, along with *priyaṅgu*, mustard seeds, honey, curd, and milk. (112)
Fruit, cake, and betel leaf are said to be the twenty-six substances; this is renowned as the "excellent" (uttama) offering, while that which is contained in a shell is called "middling" (madhyama).

The lowest [type] ends with Vaiṣṇava; thus it is proclaimed to be threefold. However, the fuel-sticks and the clarified butter [should be offered] with the root-mantra and the heart-mantra respectively. (114)

One should offer śāli rice and other grains with the Śiras-mantra, parched grain and barley flour with the Śikhā-mantra, mung beans and others with the Kavaca-mantra, and sesame seeds with the Netra-mantra. || 115 ||

Priyaṅgu should be offered with the Astra-mantra, while mustard seeds are offered with the Īśāna-mantra; honey should be offered with the Vaktra-mantra, and one should offer curd with the Ghora-mantra.
Milk should be offered into the fire on the left, while one should perform the oblation with fruit using the *sadyojāta* mantra;
first, however, one should offer the *gāyatrī* mantra associated with the "fruit-face" (*phalavaktra*) using the ten-syllable mantra.

Having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the end of the substances, one should especially perform first the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) as prescribed by the rules, using clarified butter from a ladle full to the brim.
One should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra and begin the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
This should take place at evening at the commencement of the festival, and in the morning for those who have slept. (119)
The period from sunrise until the sun has risen halfway up the sky is known as the morning time (prātaḥkāla);
one should likewise perform the first part of the rite during the hour preceding sunset.
O Moon, it is said that the third watch is the evening;
at the end of the cow-pen, one should offer the bali-oblation to the god of the day who steals beloveds during the festival.
The beginning of the fire-oblation (*homa*) is the fire-oblation itself, and the end of the fire-oblation is the offering of the sacrificial bali.
That which begins with the fire-oblation is declared to be for pacification (*śāntika*), while that which occurs in the middle of the fire-oblation is for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*). || 122 ||
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa), I worship with offerings; this is indeed the fruit of the time for the bali offering.
One should fashion an excellent liṅga out of food within the bali vessel.
Having invoked the Pāśupata [mantra] into the sacrificial lord, the *anna-liṅga*,
one should worship it, recite the *jyāstra* mantra, and display the *mukula* and *padma* mudrās. (124)
The offering of the sacrificial victim (balidāna) should be performed with the sounding of conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments;
it should be done before a trident or a food-liṅga, and not before one surrounded by the Vedic weapons-mantra.
On that day, an offering (bali) should first be presented even by those possessing wealth to the retinue beginning with Vṛṣa, specifically with their respective mantras. || 126 ||
Having specially placed the tridents and other implements upon the colored powder,
one should [proceed] with umbrellas, banners, and so forth, accompanied by hymns and auspicious recitations.
It was provided with incense and lamps, accompanied by offerings and rhythmic cymbals, attended by servants, and surrounded by all classes of devotees. || 128 ||

Wearing a turban and an upper garment, adorned with all ornaments, anointed with fragrance, richly decorated with flowers, and having performed the ritual imposition of the limbs (sakalīkṛta), the Ācārya [should proceed]. || 129 ||
One should especially offer the bali-oblation upon the central pedestal above the colored powder;
it should be offered by either the preceptor or the disciple, duly authorized by him.
Having abandoned the [central] stage area, one should proceed clockwise;
one should offer the bali-oblation starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna, or starting from Indra and ending with Brahmā. || 131 ||

Alternatively, one should offer the bali-oblation in accordance with the location of the village or dwelling; specifically, in a house with a western door, even for the three daily rites beginning with the morning.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the worldly deities beginning with Varuṇa and ending with Nimi; having worshipped the lords of the days upon the seat of the yantra in the nine locations.
One should offer the bali-oblation for them with their own respective mantras and the appropriate materials:
nine on the first day, eighteen on the second, and fourteen on the seventh day. (134)
The five-day rite, the three-day rite, the eleven-day rite, and likewise the six and two-fold offerings;
[these are for] Vighneśa, Bhūta, Gandharva, Sureśa, Muni, and Mādhava. (135)
These nine lords of the days are declared to be auspicious Asuras;
they consist of Bhūta, Indra, and Viṣṇu at the beginning, followed by six Suras, and the form of Brahmā.
Saying "This is for Śiva," the nine deities were thus released;
[he offered] the Nandyāvarta, pure food, sweetmeats, modakas, and ghee. || 137 ||
The offering for Vighneśvara is said to consist of a red lotus and milk-rice (pāyasa);
the offering should include plantains, sugar, and clarified butter, which is dear to Brahmā.
On the Jayantī day, rice mixed with sesame (kṛsarānna), coconut, and ghee,
combined with flowers, is declared to be the offering for the spirits (bhūtas). (139)
Turmeric rice, meat broth, pumpkin, and ghee are dear to Gandharva; jasmine flowers, wheat-based food, and the fruits of the jackfruit and mango are likewise remembered as his favorites.
It is said that for Indra, the offering (bali) consists of a *lakṣmī* flower together with *dūrvā* grass,
along with food mixed with curd, mung beans, black gram, and ghee.
An offering consisting of a lotus-root (padmakanda) is said to be the oblation for the sages (ṛṣis).
Tulasī, rice mixed with molasses, clarified butter, and the fruit of the bṛhatī plant [are likewise offered]. || 142 ||
Mālatī and karavīra, combined with ketakī flowers, as well as kṛsara, jāla, pūpa, and coconut. || 143 ||
One should offer honey mixed with molasses as an oblation to the Asuras; likewise, one should offer Āragvadha, pure food, and sinless jackfruit with clarified butter. (144)
This is declared to be dear to Śiva and is proclaimed as the substance for the *bali* offering.
In the absence of flowers, one should take whatever flowers are available and offer them as the *bali*.
One should cause cooked rice to be given to all [the deities] in the middle;
it should be one *droṇa*, half a *droṇa*, or half of that, as the portion of rice for the *bali* offering. || 146 ||
One should offer a bali-oblation for all [the deities] in the size of a hen’s egg.
Having cast the bali upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha), the wise one should enter the place of sacrifice after performing the washing of his feet and entering the interior. 148.
Having performed the sacrifice, the wise one should offer food in the appropriate place; Pūṣan should present stale flowers to Caṇḍeśa. (149)

One should perform the dismissal (visarjana) upon the pedestal of the offering (balipīṭha), on the liṅga of the deity, at its end, or following the sequence of the offering, while circumambulating. || 150 ||
Alternatively, on that day, having worshipped Gaṇeśa with devotion, having offered the sacrificial oblation, and having adorned him with ornaments, one should apply the sacred ashes. || 151 ||
One should perform the circumambulation of the village for the pacification of all obstacles.
One should properly offer the ritual sprouts (aṅkura) according to the specific rules, especially at twilight, accompanied by the Astra-mantra and joined with the devotee Caṇḍeśa. 153.
(58) It is provided with a canopy and an umbrella, accompanied by chowries and sprouts, endowed with new garments and silk, and joined with other [ornaments] as well. || 154 ||
The wise man should go to a pure place near a pond at Rāmavalmīka, or by a river, or even at a small lake; having sprinkled the ground with water while reciting the Astra-mantra. (155)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should duly worship the Goddess of the Earth;
then, having dug there with the root mantra, one should take the earth into a vessel. (156)
Furthermore, it should be maintained by a Śiva-brahmin, or even by the best of courtesans, or by others born of the four castes, or indeed by any devotees whatsoever. (157)
The best of preceptors should offer the sprouts at night according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the hoisting of the banner and the beating of the drum. (158)
In this very manner, preceded by the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
the best of mantra-knowers should cause [the rite] to be performed according to the previously stated procedure. (159)
One should prepare twenty-one *beras* made of gold, or of linen and cotton thread, placed upon a vessel of rice and preceded by a comfortable seat (*sukhāsana*).
The most excellent Guru should tie the protective thread (kautuka) at night for the sake of the procession;
having drawn a lotus, he should place an image twelve finger-breadths in length upon it.

The thread, consisting of three parts and composed of the three qualities (guṇas), should be placed in the center of the lotus; having worshipped it with the heart-mantra using perfumes and other offerings, one should place it upon the head of the disciple.
Having circumambulated the temple with all auspicious rites,
one should enter the interior of the temple and thereafter cause the proclamation of "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) and "Well-being" (Svasti) to be recited.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and betel, one should display the lotus mudrā. || 164 ||
"O Śambhu, be ever present at its conclusion.
Having thus informed [the deity] with his heart, the wise one should bind it on his right forearm. (165)
Adorned with all ornaments and honored with ritual services,
they were placed with devotion upon a chariot or a palanquin at the very beginning.
Soldiers with weapons in hand shall go in front, and he, mounted upon a horse, shall follow behind;
herds of elephants shall follow them, and multitudes of banners shall follow after those.
There were horse-machines, elephant-machines, and [images of] lions, bulls, deer, and horses; they were equipped with banners like swings, and possessed arches and rows of towers. || 168 ||
(61) Rich with songs, recitations, and beautiful dances, there were rows of Śaiva pavilions,
beginning from the horse-headed [image] and proceeding in sequence to the garlanded mechanical figures. 169.
These followers of the banners are indeed according to the previously mentioned sequence;
they are adorned with ornaments and accompanied by courtesans. || 170 ||
At the end of that, one should proceed in due order to the seats of Sukhāsana and the others,
as well as to the auspicious Śikhāsana accompanied by Umā.
The Lord of the Bull, the Destroyer of Tripura, the Dancer, Candraśekhara, Ardhanārī, Viṣṇu, Bhikṣāṭana, and Kālahan. (172)
Kaumārī situated in the middle of the Liṅga, as well as Umāmaheśvara, Caṇḍeśvara, Prasāda, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti itself. || 173 ||
Gajāri, Kaṅkāla, Arjunapradama,
Gaṅgādhara, and Ekapāda— these [twenty] in sequence, making twenty-one. (174)
Having honored and adorned them with sacrificial grass (sahatbhiḥ), the wise one should lead them away in due order:
one, two, three, five, seven, or fourteen [steps]. 175.
But when all desires reside within that [deity] among the twenty-one forms, the wise one should lead those bound by the single moon to the conclusion of the festival. 176.
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by peacock-feather fans and chowries,
at the end [of the procession] all the Pāśupatas, likewise those who observe the Great Vow (mahāvrata),
and the Mahāśaiva should proceed in front; thereafter, Brahmā should proceed.
Singers and dancers likewise should follow him in particular;
the Lord, accompanied by Śakti and adorned with all ornaments, [should proceed]. (179)
Surrounded by women and adorned with all kinds of ornaments and the like, he was graced by various umbrellas, banners, yak-tail fans, and various chowries. || 180 ||
It was accompanied by mechanical lamps, handheld lamps, and lamps on poles and tridents,
as well as banners, canopies, kettledrums, and musical instruments.
At the end, Caṇḍeśvara should go forth adorned with all ornaments;
at the conclusion of that, he should especially cause it to be proclaimed with all musical instruments.
And in front of everyone, one should proclaim a great sound;
a Śūdra should go at the end of that, and all the social classes (varṇas) should follow at the end of those.
Women, children, the elderly, and the young, endowed with devotion and with their minds fixed upon that Creator, O Lord of Gods, who go there— (184)

Having performed a slow circumambulation of the village, he should enter his abode;

All the people, honored by the bees and others, stood at the front;
all the dancers and musicians were on the left, as were the flute-player and the singer. (188)
The Ācārya stands on the left side facing all directions, mounted upon the king of elephants;
on both sides are the celestial nymphs, performing dance and song. (189)
To the rear of the god, the attendants stood in formation,
fanning him on both sides with female attendants holding chowries, fans, and other such items.
Adorned with fragrant incense, lamps, flowers, and other offerings,

Having led her out by the courtesans, one should cast her outside with her dowry;

One should perform every service, especially recollecting [the teacher] again and again;

when there is excessive rain, a great wind, or the occurrence of national calamities and the like. || 202 ||
In the event of such obstacles or upon the appearance of favor, one should offer the bali;
specifically, in the midst of the favor and the rain-cloud, one should offer the bali at the station of Brahmā.
One should offer the bali-oblation all around the boundary, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna;
then, having offered the bali on the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) in the east, one should bring the rite to completion.

Having especially worshipped Īśvara together with Śakti—

thereafter, one should worship as prescribed and offer milk-rice and other such items.

five niṣkas, one niṣka, three niṣkas, and two niṣkas.

specifically for those beginning with the Sun and ending with Saturn, in their respective order. (238)

having honored the preceptor [with gifts], one should ask for his forgiveness, saying, "May you forgive me."
Having given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability to those who have served as attendants,
one should perform the lowering of the banner at night, accompanied by a ritual bath.
Having bathed the primary liṅga and worshipped it especially, one should offer various oblations after bowing down with devotion. (241)
Having worshipped Caṇḍeśa and then dismissed him, one should again sever the base of the flagstaff with the Astra-mantra according to the prescribed rule, while the bull remains upon the flag.

At the time of dawn, under that same lunar mansion on that very day,
one should indeed perform the circumambulation of the village and other such places.
Then, having gone to the desired location, which is endowed with all ritual playfulness,
one should not perform the oblation, the preliminary consecration, and other rites, nor the offering at the sacred ford. (248)

then, having offered abundant gifts, one should provide excellent dancing, singing, and instrumental music. || 249 ||
The festival of Brahmā has been described; now hear about the festival of the Sun-day (Ārkavāra).
On a Sunday, one should especially worship Śiva in the morning according to the prescribed sequence. (250)
One should worship all the gods and especially offer oblations;
one should worship Candraśekhara with all the ritual services (upacāras).
At the end of the daily rite, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and all kinds of ornaments,
one should perform a circumambulation of the village or a circumambulation of the temple.
Having entered the interior, one should thereafter cause the ritual bathing to be performed there.
From the Sun (Arka) to the End of Birth (Ajānta), the festival beginning with Śakti is proclaimed.
Thus, whatever the preeminent one, who is free from sin and possesses great merit, performs—254.
Being completely liberated from all defects, one shall attain the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the ritual for the festival of Śiva, in the *Candrajñāna*, the *Śrīmukhatantra*.

But in the abode of Giriśa, situated between Vāyu and Varuṇa. || 1 ||
The installation of Mahālakṣmī must be performed by the most excellent preceptors,
after a statue of Lakṣmī seated upon a lotus throne has been fashioned by a master artisan.
She was golden-hued and adorned with lotuses held in both hands,
her mass of hair being sprinkled by the two frontal globes at the tips of an elephant's trunk.
Her two feet were encircled [by anklets], her eyes resembled lotus petals,
and she was especially attended on both sides by two maidens with chowries.
On an auspicious moment and a favorable day, the wise man should cause the sprouting ceremony (aṅkura) to be performed for Mahālakṣmī, the vast one, beloved of Viṣṇu, who is being fanned.
Then, having performed the Vāstuhoma in the presence of Mahālakṣmī, one should perform the Aṅgahoma with the Anuvāka beginning with "digbhyaḥ. (6)
And according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
having performed the three-day consecration (adhivāsa), [one should place] the products of the cow (gavya) along with milk into the waters.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village and entered the sacrificial hall,
he likewise performed the rite of proclaiming an auspicious day and the sprinkling with the five products of the cow.
Having specifically spread ten bhāras of grain upon the altar, and having accomplished the state of Manonmanī through the fivefold piling, || 9 ||
Having spread grains all around and drawn a lotus design with lines,
one should properly place a new water-pot, well-wrapped with an excellent thread.
One should place a new image of Lakṣmī into the jars;
having placed the nine gems and so forth, along with a coconut and mango sprouts, [into them]. (11)
Having covered [the vessel] with nine-colored cloths, one should place two bundles of kūrca grass;
[one should install] Mahālakṣmī in the central jar, and likewise Siddhi on the right.
The Guru should invoke and worship Vīryalakṣmī in the west, Vijayadāyinī in the north, and Kāryalakṣmī in the east.
The wise man, having invoked Umā, Sarasvatī, Sāvitrī, and Gāyatrī into the pitchers starting from the southeast (āgneya), should worship them.
One should worship the Śaktis of Lakṣmī around the principal pitcher;
one should worship the Niryātīs in order in the four directions on the four altars.
On the lower part, at the Umā-altar, one should worship the eight Śaktis;
the fire-rites should be performed according to rule, following the very path previously described. (16)
Having invited four Brahmins for the purpose of observation,
they should offer oblations according to the rules, individually, into nine separate sacrificial pits.
With the mantras "hiraṇyavarṇām," "gāyatrīm," "śriye," "jātaśriyam," and likewise "padmapriyā," [one should offer oblations] with mango flowers, sacrificial fuel sticks, and kuśa grass.
One should cultivate each [of the grains] five thousand times with nine types of grain,
for seven days, five days, or even three days.
The wise one should offer a thousand, ten thousand, or even one hundred and eight oblations with abundant sacrificial materials, while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra.

83) The best of Brahmins should perform [the rites] for the nine [planets] and others with fresh flowers, grains, honey, and likewise with sugar. || 21 ||
With clarified butter, oblation materials, curds, fuel-sticks joined with fruits,
one should perform [the rites] in the eastern lotus-pit with the root-mantra according to one's own qualities and so forth.
The oblation must indeed be offered specifically preceded by meditation;
at the time of the homa, [one should approach] the best of the twice-born who are devoted to the complete recitation of the Vedas.
Those devoted to the recitation of the Purāṇas should chant the Svasti-sūkta; likewise, oblations should be offered with the Īkāra-ty-anuvāka and the Sagunā.
Then, having performed the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should subsequently offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścitta*);
and even after causing the *jaya* and other [mantras] to proceed, one should complete the remainder of the fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
Having calculated the remainder of the night with Maṅgalaka and others,
at the time of dawn, the preceptor, together with the image-keepers, shall bathe.
Having performed the morning twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), the preceptor should recite the Gāyatrī mantra;
then, having entered the temple while muttering the Śrīsūkta for the sake of the virtuous, [he should proceed].
Having circumambulated and prostrated again and again,
one should meditate upon the goddess Dik-sutā with the mantra "Gandhadvārā."
Seated there facing north, he should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
the preceptor, having taken the water-pot, should proceed in front while maintaining silence.
Then the Guru, taking the image from the altar, follows after it;
having entered the temple, he places the image upon its seat.
Having placed the water-pot (kumbha) in front, the Guru sits facing north;
having restrained his breath according to the rule through exhalation, inhalation, and retention (recaka, pūraka, and kumbhaka).
Having performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the internal *mātṛkā*,
and likewise the external placement upon the image just as one has done upon oneself, the knower of distinctions [proceeds].
The patron, being joined with [the officiant], should cause the ten gifts to be given;
having performed the gift for the reception of the nine planets, it shall be "saṃbhūrika. || 33 ||
The knower of the ritual procedure should first worship the sacrifice extensively according to his means,
touching the image with the collections of mantras previously mentioned.
Having placed the Śrī-mantra upon his head and joyfully reciting the Śrīsūkta, he should then take the Śakti from the pitcher and install it within the image. || 35 ||
Having invoked [the deity] with the root mantra and meditated upon the goddess who bestows boons,
one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and the sixteen types of ritual services. (36)
Having offered excellent rice and then betel-leaf,
he should pray for his heart's desires in the presence of Mahālakṣmī.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and earrings,
as well as with cows, land, wealth, and whatever else is desired.
Having gratified his preceptor and bowed again to the officiating priests,
and likewise addressing them with words of blessing, he then satisfied the brahmins.
Rejoicing, he should go forth with his ancestors and kinsmen;
thus, whoever performs this with devotion, preceded by faith and love, [attains the highest state]. (40)
His sins are destroyed, and all prosperity comes into his hands;
having obtained wealth, grain, as well as female and male servants and a house. (41)
They shall bring about the increase of wife and sons, as well as health;
and in this world, abundant enjoyments that are difficult even for the gods to obtain. (42)
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot and wandering through the worlds and even beyond them by the grace of Śrī, one shall attain union with Śrī.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Lakṣmī," in the section concerning the Śakti within the Uttarabhāga of the Candrajñāna.

[the letters] ending in *dh*, *bh*, *v*, *l*, and likewise *m*.

Vānta, mānta, dhānta, bhānta, and thereafter lānta;

Gālava, the sages, and likewise Bṛhatī—these are to be known as the god Sadāśiva, conjoined with the power Unmanī. || 36 ||
The seed-syllable is primary; in its midst are the syllables *ā* and *u*. For the Brāhmaṇas, there are twenty steps, for each step respectively.
The syllable *sa* (sānta) joined with the syllable *dha* (dhānta) is the supreme state of the twenty [letters] and others;
having established the single middle syllable as the syllable *oṃ*, which is the Supreme Lord. || 38 ||
The *liṅga* established in the center of that is the syllable *oṃ*, the supreme state; it is said to consist of the letter *na* ending in *dh*, and the letter *ma* ending in *bh*. (39)

The mantra "namaḥ śivāya" is said to consist of the letter *va* (ending in *ta*), joined with *śi*; the letter *la* (ending in *ta*), joined with *va*; and the letter *ma* (ending in *ta*), joined with *ya*. || 40 ||
Thus ends the chapter on the Five Syllables in the Kriyāpāda of the Candrajñāna;
this is the twenty-first chapter.
(98) I shall proclaim the Ārdrā-vrata, which brings happiness to all living beings;
for the sake of protection through all auspiciousness, it shall result in the destruction of all enemies. || 1 ||
Having first performed the rite of offering seed-sprouts for nine or seven days,
one should commence the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) under the lunar mansion Mṛgaśīrṣa.
Thereafter, one should bathe Gaurī and clothe her in a white garment;
she should be adorned with all ornaments and her entire body fully decorated.
In a pavilion fully equipped with all requisites, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in due order;
having established Gaurī in its center, one should perform the tying of the auspicious thread (kautukabandhana).
On the stand and upon the rice grains, in their midst, is the thread-protector;
the attendant [is placed] on the right side.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums and with auspicious recitations for the ears.
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas and joined with dance and song,
one should then bind the protective amulet (kautuka) with the mantra of Tryambaka.
Thereafter, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented; one should properly arrange the cakes (apūpa).
Having offered incense and lamps to Hari, one should then present betel leaf (tāmbūla). || 8 ||
And on the second day, one should bathe the goddess Umā,
having adorned her with new garments as well as all her ornaments.
One should worship the Supreme Lord especially with all kinds of garlands;
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva using eight droṇas of śāli rice.
100) Having wrapped it above with a cloth, one should place salt in its center;
having established Gaurī above that... || 11 ||
Then one should worship Viśveśa on the southern side of Gaurī,
and especially worship Durgā on the left side.
Likewise, one situated near a well should prepare yellow turmeric;
it should be filled with a prastha measure of nimba leaves and joined toward the east.
Indeed, having taken Śakracūrṇa combined with turmeric and salt in a single vessel, and then likewise dūrvā grass and unbroken rice grains; || 14 ||
The most excellent preceptor should cause water to be poured three times clockwise into Gaurī’s right hand, and likewise cause powdered rice and unhusked grain to be offered.
Having taken up the milk-rice with his hand and having had the declaration of an auspicious day recited, he should perform the Ārdrā-vrata.
The preceptor, acting as the guide, should cause the water to be taken by grasping the hand;
then, taking turmeric and rice, he should perform the supreme act of showing [the deity].
Having placed the color of *kūrca* on the lotus-feet, rice (*vrīhi*) at the region of the navel, turmeric (*rajanī*) on the heart, and salt (*lavaṇa*) at the region of the throat; 18.
The first syllable should be placed upon the head; one should cause Manonmanī to be bestowed there.
One should worship the preceptor with sacred threads, gold, and finger-rings.
One should honor the Brahmins there, and one should also worship them well with sesame seeds;
[the rite] should be accompanied by conchs and drums, and joined with dance and song.
Having taken up the milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the hands of the attendants,
and having performed the circumambulation of the village, as well as auspicious rites upon their hands; (21)
One should perform the Ārdrā-vrata as well as the Nṛtālaṃkāra;
there should be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) at night, and perform the consecration at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
One should perform the ablution with the twenty-five [substances] and worship the Dancing Form well;
having wrapped it in a cloth, it should be adorned with all ornaments. (23)
Having adorned [the deity] with all kinds of flowers, one should anoint it with all types of perfumes;
thereafter, one should offer food offerings and present betel leaf.
Accompanied by the sound of conchs, joined with dance and song, endowed with the resonance of the Vedas, and filled with the sound of hymns of praise. || 25 ||
"Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should enter the temple.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the Ādrā-vrata, in the *Candrajñāna-pratiṣṭhā-tantra*.
Śrī said: O best of the twice-born, I shall describe how one should worship on Śivarātri during the Kṛta,
Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas.
Having worshipped him in every age, Guha should perform sacrifice in the Kṛta age;
in the Tretā age, the creator of obstacles should be worshipped; and in the Dvāpara age, one should sacrifice to Acyuta.
In the Kali age, Hara is worshipped by Brahmā, Indra,
and the sages on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha and on the second day of Phālguna.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra, the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha, the third day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, and the eighth and fifth days of Āṣāḍha; || 4 ||
On the twelfth lunar day under Śravaṇa, on the fifth under Pūrvāṣāḍhā,
on the seventh under Revatī, and on the eighth of the dark fortnight under Kṛttikā.
On the twelfth day of Mārgaśīrṣa, and likewise on the eighth day of the month of Puṣya—
having thus worshipped throughout the year, let Śivarātri be observed.
The Śivarātri on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha yields that same fruit;
however, when there is an excess of nights within a single month or two fortnights, that [latter] one is indeed superior.
By worshipping Śiva there with these two, a man obtains that fruit;
he should maintain a steady pace for a fortnight, especially during the first part of the night.
If the night is the longer half [of the lunar day], the worship of Śiva is prescribed;
that night shall be Śivarātri, and in this way, his very presence [is attained]. || 9 ||
That night during the waning fortnight is remembered as being full of defects,
especially with respect to each watch (yāma) due to the particular importance of the worship of Śiva.
On the ninth day and also on the seventh day, perform the rite of offering sprouts;
thereafter, one should offer the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure.
On the day prior to that, however, one should again purify the pavilion;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then tie the protective thread (kautuka).
Having fully worshipped the bilva leaf endowed with all fragrances, the wise man should wrap it in cloth; this is the consecration (adhivāsana) of the bilva leaf.
The wise teacher should perform his bath in the Prabhāpavimala [tīrtha];
he should perform libations in the forenoon and circumambulation at midday.
Having performed worship in the evening, one should likewise observe the vow;
for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras should do so while joined with fasting. (15)
[He prescribed] fasting for all twice-born ones who are devotees of Śiva, for all living beings as well,
and likewise for all women.
Free from sleep, one should accomplish all tasks with diligent effort;
likewise, one shall obtain good fruit, all perfections, and whatever is desired. || 17 ||
It bestows longevity, spiritual accomplishment, and complete liberation;
even by worshipping it when inauspicious, one becomes most auspicious in future births. (18)
Even one who was previously without a wife, having worshipped [on this day], becomes endowed with a wife again;
indeed, by worshipping on Śivarātri, one obtains the fruit of all desired objects.
The fruit of sleep is inferior, yet the fruit of being without sleep is great;
therefore, with every effort, one should observe a fast while remaining awake. (20)
The preceptor should perform worship with the four Vedas— the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan— at each watch of the day, together with Brahmā, Indra, and the sages.
One should first worship Vighneśa, and after that, the worship of the Sun;
having prepared rice from śāli grains, one should then cause the proclamation of the auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
In the first [bath] there should be the five products of the cow; in the second, there should be the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having bathed [the deity] with honey in the third, one should use the essence of sugarcane in the fourth.
The supreme guide should perform worship especially during each watch (yāma).
In the first watch, however, bathing is prescribed; one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
In the second [rite], the ceremonial bath is prescribed; it should consist of fifty pitchers.
In the third, the ceremonial bath likewise consists of twenty-five in number. (25)
In the fourth [watch], one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship with nine jars;
the wise person should especially cause the bath to be performed during every watch.
Having worshipped in the southeast, one should honor [the deity] with bilva leaves;
in the second [direction] with leaves and flowers, and in the third with jasmine flowers.
Having worshipped with *nandyāvarta* flowers, one should worship during the four watches;
one should perform the worship at the four twilights accompanied by *bilva* leaves.
On the first day, there should be food consisting of mung beans; on the second, milk-rice (pāyasa);
on the third, kṛsara rice; and on the fourth, pure rice.
One should especially worship the Guardian of the Field (kṣetrapāla) at each watch;
at the end of the watch, however, one should especially perform the bali-offering and the fire-sacrifice (homa). (30)
There, one should worship the guide with garments, gold, and rings;
there, one should honor a Brahmin and properly worship those who are devotees of Śiva.
One should honor the attendants with garments, gold, and rings;
[this rite] brings prosperity, victory, merit, and increases longevity and health. (32)
Having thus worshipped according to the rules, one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the ritual procedure for the vow of Śivarātri, in the Candrajñāna [Tantra].
Śrī said:
"O Bṛhaspati, hereafter I shall explain the offering of the bali-oblation."
For the purpose of destroying all diseases, it shall bring about total pacification. || 1 ||
It brings prosperity to the village, is meritorious, bestows all sovereignty, is dear to all the gods, and destroys famine in the kingdom. (2)

The offering of oblations (balidāna) consists of these five types in their respective order: that of the Self-born (Svāyambhuva), the divine (daivika), that of the sages (ārṣa), that of the Gaṇas (gāṇapa), and the human (mānuṣa). || 3 ||
It was provided with all kinds of musical instruments, adorned with every ornament, filled with various lamps, and surrounded by courtesans and others.
One should worship the river Gaṅgā on the right side of the door, and one should worship Kālā Yamunā on the left side of the door. || 5 ||
Having worshipped Ṛṣabha in the east and Sāgastya in the south-eastern quarter,
one should worship Bhṛṅgarāja in the south, accompanied by the group of the Seven Mothers.
One should offer oblations with their respective mantras to Lamboṣṭha and Vīrabhadra;
likewise, one should offer to Vināyaka in the southwest and to Ṣaṇmukha in the west.
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā in the northwestern direction, and likewise worship Soma on the path; one should worship Bhānu in the northeast, and similarly, Bhūtanātheśa at the front.
Having offered an oblation in the first [enclosure] and especially in the second,
one should proceed to the gate accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and the blaring of conchs.
One should especially worship the most excellent serpent at each door;
likewise Indra, Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.
Vāruṇa and Vāyu, Soma and Īśāna;
Nirṛti in the south, Viṣṇu and Brahmā in the northeast and northwest respectively. (11)
Between Soma and Śaṅkara, one should worship Kṣetrapāla;
this is the [daily] rite for the Lord of the Field.
The second enclosure has been described; now hear of the third enclosure: Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and Ekanetraka. (13)
