Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin—this is declared the third enclosure; now hear of the fourth enclosure. (14)
Here, Śiva, Paśupati, Rudra, and likewise Bhava;
Īśāna, Mahādeva, and Bhīma as the eighth—thus [are they]. (15)
The fourth enclosure has been described; now hear of the fifth enclosure:
the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, as well as the noose and the goad. (16)
The mace, the trident, [the discus], and the lotus—these constitute the ten weapons.
Thus, the enclosure and the great pedestal are each distinct. (17)
Beginning with the first case-ending and ending with the third, this is the Śāmbarī-bali-pīṭhaka;
having offered the bali separately in each location, one should likewise perform the threefold enclosure.
And in the second great seat, one should offer an oblation to the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti).
One should cause the Great Element to be placed upon the pericarp, which has five faces;
[then] the image, the enclosure, the pedestal, and the great pedestal... || 20 ||
The second enclosure is deficient in the first *bhūtapīṭha*. (21)
Having performed the bali offering specifically, it is classified as superior, middling, or inferior; this is declared to be the deity of the bali. Now, listen to the substances for the bali.
The bali offering, accompanied by food and endowed with the king of mantras;
the nourishing rite (pauṣṭika), the food-liṅga, the pacifying rite (śāntika), and likewise the water-offering (arghya). || 23 ||
Alternatively, [one may offer] the bali-offering to the Lord of the Weapon (Astrarāja), or indeed to the Preceptor (Deśika), or likewise [to others].
One should offer six droṇas of incense, twelve droṇas of flowers, and one droṇa of leaves.
What is called "balidravya" refers to the offering of bali with the utterances of svāhā and svadhā;
one should perform the bali offering at the three junctions of the day: morning, midday, and evening.
One should not perform the ritual sequence of the bali offering at any other times of day except for the sandhyās;
having performed the bath according to the rules, one should wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and white garments.
The supreme instructor, the Guru, should wear a turban and an upper garment;
with his hand holding a pavitra, he should hold the vessel for the arghya offering.
Having summoned an attendant,
he [should place] a turban and an upper garment upon the image of Candraśekhara, whether on a vehicle or in a painting.
Having placed it upon one's own head, one should perform the ritual circumambulation;
having performed the sprinkling and purification, especially for the servant of the deity.
p.
116) Furthermore, the preceptor, the best of teachers and knower of mantras, having consecrated the disciple again with these [waters],
should sprinkle him with perfume using the mantra "gandhadvārām" while applying only six drops.
One should worship the flower above the pericarp with its own name-mantra;
having offered water for the feet (pādya), one should again cause the water for honor (arghya) to be given with the arghya mantras.
Then, having displayed the incense mudrā,
one should display the lamp mudrā by joining the thumb and ring finger in succession with the thumb and forefinger.
With the mantra, one should perform the trident-mudrā (śūlamudrā), especially during the offering of the bali;
then, having offered water once more, one should perform the rite known as the salutation (namaskāra).
All the ritual offerings (upacāras), especially those of the second [category],
or even another set of offerings, should be cast as an oblation (bali) after setting them apart individually.
At the time of the offering, one should look toward the Gaṇas and the Lord;
one should especially cause the offering to be given in a pure place, and indeed everywhere. (36)
If the fifth enclosure is deficient, one should provide the second enclosure;
if the second enclosure is deficient, especially the first. || 37 ||
On the great seat (mahāpīṭha) joined with a single enclosure, the wise one should cast the offering (bali); upon that flower, he should [worship] Durgā. || 38 ||
Having thus performed the circumambulation and having taken up the covered alms-bowl, one should enter through the door of the householder and wash one's feet. (39)
Having joined the primary image with the form of Candraśekhara,
one should then offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), and the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana).
Having worshipped with fragrances, flowers, and so forth, one should likewise perform the rites ending with the lamp.
Having thoroughly worshipped the primary image (mūlabera), one should perform the ritual of reconnection (pratisandhi). || 41 ||
O Bṛhaspati, what was described as the eastern gate applies to the west as well;
however, there is indeed some slight distinction regarding everything stated for the eastern gate.
At the conclusion of the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), the preceptor should worship the deities of the bali offering;
he should present the bali to each one individually, or perhaps accompanied by a bell.
One should offer oblations to the two Nandīs on the right and left of the deity;
having worshipped the bull in front, one should worship Durgā in the north-western direction.
Having worshipped Jyeṣṭhā in the north (Saumya), and the Sun in the northeast (Aiśānya);
and having worshipped Agastya in the southeast (Vahni) within the portion of the disc (Cakrasya-aṃśe).
To the south, one should worship Bhṛṅgarāja together with the group of the Seven Mothers,
as well as Vighneśa and Vīrabhadra, having offered the bali-oblation in the proper sequence. (46)
Having especially offered a bali-oblation to Vināyaka in the southwest, the first enclosure (āvaraṇa) is declared; now hear about the second enclosure.
Furthermore, having offered the scattered oblation (vikira) with the two gatekeepers of the gopura,
one should worship Varuṇa in the west and Vāyu in the northwest.
Having propitiated Soma in the region of Soma, one should worship Īśa;
having propitiated Indra in the region of Indra, one should worship Vahni in the region of Vahni. || 49 ||
Having worshipped Yama in the southern direction, and likewise worshipping Nirṛti;
[he should worship] Viṣṇu in the south and Brahmā in the north-eastern corner of Īśa.
Or one should offer the bali-oblation accompanied by the soma-plant, using their respective mantras;
especially in the great *pīṭha*, [one should offer it] on the tips of the petals of the *cāmōda* and other [flowers]. (51)
One should place the great element upon the pericarp at the five faces;
having thus performed the circumambulation toward the deity Varuṇa. (52)
Having brought [the deity] to the doorway, perform the washing of the feet;
having worshipped the bali-offering, one should then present the collyrium for the eyes.
O Bṛhaspati, one should perform the offering of the bali at the three junctions of the day;
if it is performed otherwise, there will be calamity for the kingdom in this world.
One should then perform daily festivals accompanied by offerings;
for without a daily festival, the deity does not bestow prosperity upon the village. (55)
That village and the king’s realm shall undoubtedly prosper; and those men who perform circumambulation during the procession of the Nityotsava— (p. 121) —[shall likewise prosper].
They provide constant happiness, and one shall attain the world of Śiva;
thus, by worshipping with devotion, one attains union (sāyujya) at the end. || 57 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the ritual procedure for the offering of oblations (*balidānavidhi*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Candrajñāna*.
Henceforth I shall proclaim the impurity of the twice-born; listen now.
Regarding birth-impurity and death-impurity, purification is said to occur after ten days. (1)
If a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage shall indeed perform the funeral rites;
however, for ten days, this applies to the father, and if there is a grandson, it applies to him as well as to the brothers.
In the fourth [generation], there should be ten nights; for a male in the fifth, six nights;
in the sixth, purification occurs after four days; but in the seventh, it is three days. (3)
For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), there is indeed impurity for the giver;
if there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that it applies to the wife as well. (4)
Alternatively, I shall explain in another way in brief:
the period of impurity is prescribed for that son who has been given away by his parents.
In due course, he no longer shared in the impurity or the funeral meals with his kinsmen;
for in childhood, apart from his parents, the noble donor alone performed the rites for him there. (6)
He alone would be one who has taken up the aforementioned burden; now his sin is described:
if he then forms a connection with another's lineage, being without parents, in that former family. (7)
Indeed, whatever ritual action the disciple undertakes, the attendants of the preceptor, and the patron perform that ritual action first, [preceded by] the *pūrva* [rite]. 8.
Then, having performed the ritual bath with cow products, one should carry out the remaining rites;
afterwards, one should observe the period of impurity according to the sequence of the appropriate days.
If [an impurity] should arise at any time for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, ascetics, or celibate students, one should observe the period of impurity accordingly.
(125) If one does not possess the lineage of the ritual acts beginning with consecration (saṃskāra), then one should have them performed; one should carry out those ritual acts oneself. || 11 ||

Afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the ritual bath with cow-products and offered the cow-products [as oblation], one should again cause all the rites to be performed; of this there is no doubt.
When impurity due to death has arisen, the case of birth-impurity occurs as follows:
birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity does not purify birth-impurity. (13)
One purified by a birth-impurity is purified by another birth-impurity, and one purified by a death-impurity by another death-impurity.
Regarding the five-day period and so forth beginning from the start of the Kalpa, it should proceed for ten days; the movement follows the directions.
If [the impurity] occurs on the final day of the first period, one is purified at dawn by the second period according to the sequence.
(126) Thus has been declared the impurity for the twice-born; now hear the impurity for the Kṣatriya.
For both birth-impurity and death-impurity, the pure one [remains so] for twelve days. (14 1/2)
If a son is born in one's own lineage, those of that same lineage should observe the period of impurity;
likewise, if a daughter is born, it applies to the father and his own kin.
In the case of a male birth, purification occurs after eleven nights on the fifth day of the week, after five days on the sixth, and after four days on the seventh. (16½)
For those who have entered another lineage, the inheritance and the period of impurity are likewise determined;
if there is impurity for the husband, there is certainly impurity for the wife as well—of this there is no doubt. (17½)
Alternatively, I shall explain in brief according to another method:
the period of impurity is prescribed for a son who is an adopted son (dattrima). || 18½ ||

In due course, she had no contact with her relatives during the period of impurity; nor did she have any contact with her parents in childhood, other than with the one who performed their duties for them. (19½)
He alone shall be the great remover of disease; thus his lineage is now described.
He has no connection with a previous family line, nor does he have any affliction from his parents. (20½)
From the time the disciple begins the ritual action as an attendant of the preceptor until the completion of the rite, the patron shall observe the impurity that has arisen. (21½)
Then, having performed the cow-bath (gavyasnāna), one should carry out the remaining rites;
thereafter, one should observe the period of impurity (āśauca) for the appropriate number of days in sequence.
If [an impurity] should arise at any time for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, ascetics, or celibate students, one should observe the period of impurity accordingly.

If those who have not undergone the preparatory rites and so forth do not possess their own lineage, one should cause them to perform the preparatory rites and carry out those very actions once again. (24½)
Afterwards, having performed the ninefold bath and the *gavya* rite on an inauspicious day, one should again perform all the rituals; of this there is no doubt. (25½)

When impurity arising from a corpse has occurred, whatever initial [impurity] may have been present is purified by that corpse-impurity; however, birth-impurity is not purified by the purifications for a corpse or a corpse-birth.
Impurity from birth is purified by one who has given birth, and impurity from death is purified by one who has suffered a death.
From a short period, one may go for five days and so forth, up to ten days;
below ten days...
[omitted] ...if, on the final day of the former [period],... [omitted]...
On the morning of the second day, after three days have passed, [she becomes] pure. || 28 ||
This [period] should be increased by one, two, or three days starting from half a day;
this is declared to be the impurity for Kṣatriyas. Now hear about the impurity for cognate relatives (jñāti). || 29 ||
One becomes pure after thirteen days from both birth-impurity and death-impurity;
if a son is born within the same lineage (gotra), one should perform the rites for that lineage.
If there is a daughter for a father, it lasts thirteen days; for those born together [brothers], it is four days; for a son, it is ten days; and on the eighth day, it is five days for a male.
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after six days; in the seventh, after five days, in due order.
For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), the impurity lasts for ten days.
If there is impurity for the husband, there is undoubtedly impurity for the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.
For one whose son has died while fighting, purification is ordained;
however, there is no period of impurity for him to observe in sequence along with his kinsmen. (34)
He who, having been given away by his parents in childhood to another, performs labor there, shall be considered a stealer of wealth; that very case is now being described. (25)
How can there be a connection with one's former lineage or with one's parents? For the disciple, having begun his ritual duties, becomes an attendant to the teacher. (36)
If impurity arises again for the sacrificer due to the completion of a ritual act,
he should then perform a bath with cow-products and carry out the remainder of the rite.
Of those who have been initiated, those established in their vows, ascetics, and celibate students. || 38 ||
If at the time [of the birth] something has arisen, one should observe impurity accordingly;
131) furthermore, if there is no one of one's own lineage for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*), [the following applies]. 39.

He should cause the purificatory rites and other such acts to be performed, and carry out those rituals; subsequently, on an auspicious day, having performed the "cow-day" rite (*gavyadina*) and the cow-bath (*gavyasnāna*), as well as the *puṇyāha* ceremony.
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed, even when impurity due to death has arisen, just as in the case of postpartum impurity. || 41 ||
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity does not purify death-impurity;
one affected by birth-impurity is purified only by birth-impurity, and one affected by death-impurity is purified by death-impurity. || 42 ||
From the few days, one should go for ten days starting from the day of the snake;
if on the final day of the former [period], it is from two days.
When pure, at dawn, after three days... || 43 ||
From half a day onwards, this [period of impurity] may increase by two or three days.
Thus the impurity arising from birth has been declared; now hear the impurity pertaining to the *garīka* and *gaṇīkā*. (44)
Impurity due to birth is purified after fourteen days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage should perform the funeral rites.
If the daughter dies on the tenth day, it is the fourth [impurity] for those born together;
if the fifth [day] falls within nine days, it shall be thirteen nights.
In the case of those who have entered another gotra, one should observe the impurity for six days; furthermore, the impurity lasts for only one day.
There is no doubt that whatever impurity (āśauca) does not affect the husband does not affect the wife either;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.
(133) For the fourth [initiation], impurity is ordained;
however, there is no sequence for him regarding impurity together with his kinsmen. || 49 ||

He who was given away by his two mothers in childhood to another, yet remains there performing labor for them, shall be entitled to a share of gold; likewise, the sin [of such an act] is now described.
Even for one born of a noble lineage, when deprived of his parents,
his disciples indeed begin the rites as attendants of the preceptor.
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the patron of the sacrifice,
he should perform a bath with cow-products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity and perform bathing in due order;
this applies likewise to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and yogis as well. (53)

If, at the time [of birth], that which has arisen [is a son]—one should observe impurity accordingly; provided there is no other [son] of one's own lineage for the sake of the sacramental rites and other ceremonies. (54)
One should have the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) performed and carry out those specific rituals;
afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (gavyasnāna) and the rite for a holy day (puṇyāha), [one should proceed].
Furthermore, one should perform all ritual duties without any doubt, even when impurity due to death has arisen, just as one would during the period of birth-impurity. || 56 ||
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by the purifications for birth-impurity;
a woman in childbirth is purified only by another birth-impurity, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity. (57)
From five days [of illness], one should recover in ten days; from ten days, in the same time [ten days].
If it occurs on the first or the last day, recovery is in two and a half days; if at dawn, in three days.
From this point on, one should increase [the period] by one, two, or three days starting from half a day.
The impurity for a female attendant of Rudra has been declared; now hear the impurity for a temple servant girl (devadāsī). (59)
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified in ten days and five days respectively;
if a son is born in one's own lineage, that lineage must perform the funeral rites.
If a daughter is born on the fifteenth day, [the impurity] for those born together with that deity lasts fourteen nights; if it is the fifth day within the ten-day period, [it lasts] ten days.
In the sixth generation, purification occurs after ten days; in the seventh, after seven days, respectively.
This applies to those who have entered another gotra, as well as regarding inheritance and impurity.
When the husband undergoes impurity due to death, the wife also shares in that portion; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief. (63)
(136) "The son who delivers his mother from [the womb] is ordained to observe her impurity;
however, he had no impurity in due order with respect to his kinsmen. (64)
If, during childhood, one steals from others what belongs to the two parents, he shall be the one who takes it back; that sin is now being described. (65)
When, however, there is no connection by a prior lineage with the two mothers, then the disciples and the attendants of the preceptor shall indeed begin the ritual action. (66)
If, after the completion of the sacrificer's rites, a period of impurity (āśauca) should arise again,
then, having performed a bath with cow-products (gavya), he should carry out the remaining ritual acts.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards, according to the sequence of the appropriate days;
this applies likewise to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and to yogins.
If at the time [of the rite] something has arisen that renders one impure, one should observe that period of impurity;
subsequently, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products and a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa), [one may proceed]. (69)
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed when impurity due to death has arisen,
just as in the case of birth-impurity.

Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for purifying death-impurity; likewise, one affected by birth-impurity is purified by another case of birth-impurity, and one affected by death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself.
From a short period, the transition from one daśā to another occurs after ten days plus five more;
if it is on the day of the end of the previous [daśā], it occurs after two days, or at dawn, after three days when purified.
From this point on, one should increase [the offerings] by one, two, or three [units] starting from half a day.
The teachers, deities, and female attendants are assigned according to the procedure stated for the male practitioners.
p.
138) Those belonging to the lineage of liberation, however, should not practice sin against one another; having abandoned this scripture, one should not contemplate any other scripture. (74)
The impurity for a temple servant woman has been declared; now hear about the impurity of those not related by marriage.
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified from the eyes in due order. (75)
If a son is born, the rite should be performed by one of his own lineage;
if it is a daughter, it should be performed by another of that lineage for fifteen days, or at that very time for those born together with her.
If the fifth [lunar day] falls within the first ten days, it shall be fourteen nights;
for those on the sixth and so on, purification occurs sequentially after seven days.
For those who have entered another lineage, both the inheritance and the period of impurity belong to the husband;
if the husband is subject to impurity, there is no doubt that the wife is as well. (78)
Alternatively, I shall explain in another way in brief:
for the son who is the giver [of the gift], the impurity of that [gift] is prescribed for the son. (79)

His period of ritual impurity was not shared with his kinsmen in the usual manner; rather, it was observed by his two parents during his childhood, as he had been given away elsewhere to be raised by one who performed his duties for him.
He alone would be the one who carries away the bear; now the sin resulting from that is being described.
There is never any kinship with the ancestors in the lineage of the East (Pūrvagotra) except through the parents. 81.
If impurity should arise before the disciple has commenced the rites, or while the officiating priest, the assistant priests, the patron, or the ritual son are engaged in the performance; || 82 ||
Then, having performed the ritual bath with cow products (gavya), one should carry out the remaining rites;
thereafter, one should observe the period of impurity (āśauca) until the appropriate day arrives in due course.

In the same way, if [death] should occur at any time for those who have been initiated, for those established in their vows, or likewise for yogins, one should observe impurity (āśauca) accordingly. (84)
If, however, the initiatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth do not exist within one's own lineage, one should have those rites performed and carry out those actions accordingly. (85)
Afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the ritual bath with cow products and the sprinkling, one should again cause all the rites to be performed; of this there is no doubt. (86)
When impurity due to death has arisen, the case of birth-impurity occurs as follows:
birth-impurity is purified by the rites for the dead, and death-impurity is purified by the rites for birth. (87)
A woman who has recently given birth is purified by another woman who has recently given birth, and corpses are purified by another corpse.
141) If [the period] exceeds five days but is less than ten days, the arrival of the ten-day impurity shall apply. || 88 ||
On the final day of the first [fortnight], during the morning of the second half-day, after three days have passed;
from this point, beginning with half a day, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, and three [days] in sequence. || 89 ||
The impurity pertaining to the Pāraśavas has been declared; now hear concerning the impurity of the Māheśvaras.
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified in nine days and ten days respectively, in due order.
If a son is born, one belonging to that same lineage should perform [the rites];
if it is a daughter, then fifteen days [are required] for those born together with her.
If the fifth day falls within the ten-day period, it shall be fourteen nights;
but if one becomes pure suddenly on the sixth, then on the seventh, it is seven days according to the sequence.
For those who have entered another lineage, both the inheritance and the period of impurity belong to the husband;
if the husband is in a state of impurity, the wife is likewise so—of this there is no doubt. (93)
Alternatively, I shall explain in another way in brief:
for the son of a father who is a *yodatri*, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed as follows.
He had no period of ritual impurity (āśauca) shared with his kinsmen in due course;
for he had been given away by his parents while still an infant to another, where he performed his duties.
He alone would be one who has ascended the necklace; likewise, the sin is now described:
when there is no connection with the former lineage, nor ever with the parents, yet the disciple, having commenced the rites, becomes an attendant upon the teacher. (96)
If impurity should arise for the sacrificer before the completion of the rite,
he should then perform a bath with cow-products and carry out the remaining ritual actions.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards, according to the sequence of the appropriate days;
this applies likewise to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise to yogins. (98)
If at the time [of the birth] something has occurred, one should observe that period of impurity;
however, if there is no one of one's own lineage (gotra) for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (saṃskāra), [the following applies]. 99.
One should have the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) performed and carry out those specific rituals;
afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the ritual bath with cow products (gavyasnāna) and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if there were the impurity of childbirth. || 101 ||

A birth-impurity is purified by a death-impurity, but a death-impurity is not purified by the rites for birth; one who has given birth is purified only by another birth-impurity, and a death-impurity is purified by a death-impurity. 102.
From a short [period], there is purification after five days;
if it occurs on the final day of the previous [period], then after two days; if it is pure at dawn, then after three days. (103)
From this point, one should increase the period by one, two, or three days starting from half a day;
this is declared to be the impurity for a Māheśvara. Now hear the impurity for a Vaiśya.
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are purified in ten days and seven days respectively;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, a member of that lineage should indeed perform the purification rites.
If the daughter [is born] on the fifteenth day, that very [period] belongs to those born together;
and if the fifth [lunar day] falls within the ten-day period, it would belong to him.
In the sixth month, purification occurs immediately; in the seventh, it is after seven days in succession.
For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), there is both inheritance and the period of impurity.
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that there is also [impurity] for the wife.
Or else, I shall explain in another way, in brief: (108)
The impurity prescribed for that son who gives away his daughter is not shared by his kinsmen; rather, it applies to him alone in due order. || 109 ||
He who performs ritual acts there during childhood under the care of his parents shall be one whose [sin] has been uprooted; likewise, the sin [of such a person] is now being described.
There is never any kinship with the ancestors of one's former lineage; for once the disciple has begun the rites, he becomes an attendant of the teacher. (111)
If impurity arises for the sacrificer before the completion of the ritual act,
he should then perform a bath with cow products and proceed with the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then it will be an unsuitable day for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise for yogis. (113)

If at the time [of birth] something has occurred, one should observe impurity accordingly; furthermore, if there is no one of one's own lineage for the rites of consecration and so forth, [the same applies]. (114)

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products (*gavya*) and a ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed,
even when impurity due to death has arisen, provided that [the following] occurs.
Birth-impurity is purified by [the end of] the period of death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by the means used for birth-impurity;
one who has given birth is purified only by the [end of] the birth-impurity period, and death-impurity is purified by [the end of] the death-impurity period. (117)
If the planets are in the *dāśābhāga*, one should calculate five days and so forth up to ten days from the [remaining] small portion.
If, on the final day of the previous [period], they are purified by two days, then at dawn they are purified by three days. (118)
The period of impurity for a Vaiśya has thus been declared; now hear the period of impurity for a Śūdra. (119)
Impurity due to birth or impurity due to death is purified in one month;
however, if a son is born within one's own lineage, one should observe that rigorous procedure.
If a daughter is born within one month [of the father's death], then for those who are co-born (sapinda), there shall be the fifteen-day period of impurity;
on the eleventh day, it shall be the fifth day [of impurity].

Or, purification occurs on the sixth day for a Śūdra; for those who have entered another lineage (gotra), the inheritance and the period of impurity follow the respective order of the seven [castes] and the eight days. 122.
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that it exists for the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief.

(148) Regarding the son who is a *dātrima* (given-away) son, his period of impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed; however, he had no impurity in common with his paternal kinsmen, according to the sequential rule. || 124 ||

He who was given away by his parents to another during childhood and performs work for that person is called a *rūḍhahārī*; now, the *agha* (the one who takes what is not given) is described. || 125 ||
There is never any connection with one's former lineage when apart from one's parents;
for once the rites have begun, the disciple indeed becomes an attendant of the teacher.
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the sacrificer,
he should perform a bath with cow products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity (āśauca) afterwards, according to the sequence of the appropriate days;
and the same applies to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise to yogis.

If, at the time [of birth], that which has arisen [is a son]—one should observe impurity accordingly; provided, however, that for the rites such as the purificatory ceremonies (*saṃskāra*), there is no one of one's own lineage (*svagotra*). (129)

One should cause the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (gavyasnāna) and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if it were the impurity of childbirth. || 131 ||

A birth-impurity is purified by a death-impurity, but a death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurities; one who is impure from birth is purified by another birth-impurity, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. 132.

If one travels for a short period of ten days plus five, or if the journey takes place after the tenth day, then on the final day of the first period, one is purified by two days; if it is at dawn, then by three days. (133)
(150) From half a day onwards, one should increase [the period] by a sequence of one, two, and three [days].
This is declared to be the impurity for Śūdras; now hear the impurity for Karakolas. || 134 ||
Impurity due to birth or death is purified after thirty days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, that lineage must perform the purificatory rite.
If the daughter dies on the thirty-fourth day, then for those born together [in the same birth-year], there shall be impurity for sixteen nights; and if on the twelfth day, it lasts for five days.
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after ten days; in the seventh, it is nine days, in due order.
For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), both the inheritance and the period of impurity (āśauca) apply.
If there is a husband, there is also a wife; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief. (138)
p.

151) Regarding the son who is a *dātrima* (given son), the impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for him is as follows: his impurity was shared with his [adoptive] kinsmen, and it did not persist according to the [biological] sequence. || 139 ||
One who, having been given away by his parents in childhood to another, performs work there, is known as a *rūḍhahārī*; likewise, the *aghamarṣaṇa* is now described. (140)
There is never any kinship with the ancestors of one’s former lineage; for once the disciple has begun the rites, he becomes an attendant of the preceptor. (141)
If an impurity arises during the completion of a ritual act for a sacrificer,
he should then perform a bath with cow products and carry out the remainder of the rite.
If one's own lineage for the rites of consecration and so forth does not exist, then one should have them performed by another and carry out those ritual actions oneself. || 143 ||
p.

152) Afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the ritual bathing with cow products and the sprinkling, one should again cause all the rites to be performed; of this there is no doubt. || 144 ||
When impurity arising from a corpse occurs while one is already in the state of birth-impurity, the birth-impurity is purified by the corpse-impurity;
however, the birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for purifying a corpse. (145)
If one departs from a short distance, one may travel ten days, provided it exceeds five days; from ten days, the journey [is extended].
If on the final day of the former [period], [the purification occurs] on the second day, then at dawn, after three days, when it is pure. 146.
From this point on, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, or three half-days at a time.
The purification for Kārakola has been declared; now hear the purification for Bhaṭṭārya. || 147 ||
Regarding the impurity caused by birth or death, however, one becomes pure after thirty days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage should indeed perform the purificatory rite.

If the daughter [is born] on the thirty-fourth day, then for those of equal status (sahaja), the impurity (agha) lasts for sixteen nights; if it is the son, it lasts ten days, and on the fifth day, he becomes eligible [for rites]. (149)

For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), purification occurs after six days for the first, ten days for the second, and nine days for the third, in due order; this applies both to inheritance and to impurity (āśauca).
If there is impurity for the husband, there is undoubtedly impurity for the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.

Regarding the son who was given away as a *dātrima*, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for him was observed by his own kinsmen; however, there was no such impurity for him in relation to [his biological] family members in due order. 152.

One who, having been given away by his parents during childhood to another, performs work for that person, is known as a *rūḍhahārī*; now, the *agha* (the one who takes what is not given) is described. (153)
(154) At what time is there a connection with one's former lineage, even in the absence of parents?
For it is by undertaking ritual actions that the disciple becomes an attendant of the teacher. 154.
If impurity should arise for the sacrificer before the completion of the rite,
he should then perform a bath with cow-products and proceed with the remainder of the ritual.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, in due order, one may perform the rite on a suitable day.
This applies likewise to those who have received initiation, those established in vows, and yogis as well. (156)
If at the time [of the birth] something has arisen, one should observe impurity accordingly;
having performed the daily rites, if there is no one of one's own lineage remaining, [then one should perform the funeral rites]. 157.

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products (*gavya*) and a ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if there were birth-impurity. (159)
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for cleansing death-impurity;
one who has given birth is purified only by another birth-impurity, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. (160)
If ten days pass with five days remaining, it is the *daśāhagama* [impurity];
if on the final day of the former period, it is from two days; if on a pure morning, it is from three days. || 161 ||
From this point on, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, or three half-days starting from half a day.
This is declared to be the impurity for the Bhaṭṭāryas; now hear the impurity for the Śālis. || 162 ||
Regarding the impurity caused by birth or death, one becomes pure after thirty-four days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage must perform the purificatory rite (agha).

If it is a daughter on the thirty-fourth day, then for those born at the same time, there shall be impurity for sixteen nights; and on the twelfth day, it is the fifth [day of the lunar fortnight]. (164)
In the sixth generation, purification occurs after ten days; in the seventh, after nine days, respectively.
This applies to those who have entered another lineage (gotra), as well as regarding inheritance and impurity (āśauca).
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that there is also impurity for the wife;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.
The period of impurity prescribed for a son given away by his parents is ordained;
however, he had no impurity in common with his paternal kinsmen, according to the sequence of rules. || 167 ||
He who was given away by his parents to another during childhood and performs work there is known as a *rūḍhahārī*; likewise, the *agha* [type] is now described. (168)
p.
157) There is no connection with one's former lineage, nor ever with one's parents; for once the rites have been commenced, the disciple indeed becomes an attendant of the teacher. (169)
If impurity arises for the sacrificer due to the completion of a ritual act,
he should then perform a bath with cow-products and proceed with the remainder of the rite.

One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, according to the sequence, one should perform the rite on an appropriate day for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise for yogins. (171)

If, at the time [of birth], twelve days of impurity (āśauca) should be observed, and if there is no one of one's own lineage (svagotra) for the performance of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) and other ceremonies; 172.

One should cause the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the bath with cow-products (gavya-snāna) and the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
Furthermore, one should cause all ritual acts to be performed without doubt,
even when impurity due to death has arisen, just as in the case of a woman who has given birth. (174)
A birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for the dead, nor is a death-impurity purified by the rites for birth;
a woman in childbirth is purified only by another woman in childbirth, and a death-impurity is purified by the rites for the dead. (175)
If one travels for more than five days but less than ten, the journey is considered completed after ten days.
If the journey begins on the last day of the previous period, one is purified after two days; if it begins on the morning of the third day, one is purified after three days.
From this point, starting from half a day, one should increase [the duration] by a sequence of one, two, and three [days].
This is declared to be the impurity for a Śālī artisan; now hear the impurity for a Śilpika artisan. || 177 ||
In the case of impurity due to birth or death, one becomes pure after thirty-five days;
however, if a son is born within one's own lineage, a member of that lineage should perform the purificatory rite.
If the daughter is fifty days old, then for those whose nature is innate (sahaja), it would be seventeen yugas and ten days; the fifth [stage] is thirteen and ten days. (179)
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after eleven days; in the seventeenth, it is by degrees [after fifteen days].
For those who have entered another lineage (gotra), this applies to both inheritance and impurity (āśauca). || 180 ||
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that there is also [impurity] for the wife;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.

For a son who has been given away by his parents, the period of impurity (āśauca) is prescribed; however, for him, there was no gradual period of impurity observed together with his paternal kinsmen. || 182 ||
If one who was given away by his parents in childhood to another becomes a performer of rites for that person, he is called a *rūḍhahārī*; that is now declared to be the lowest [type]. (183)
(160) When is there a connection with one's former lineage, yet without one's parents? For it is when the disciple, having begun the rites, becomes an attendant upon the teacher. (184)
If impurity arises for the sacrificer before the completion of the ritual act,
he should perform a bath with cow products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards, according to the sequence of unsuitable days;
this applies likewise to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and yogins.
If, at the time when [the birth] has occurred, one should observe that period of impurity;
and if, moreover, for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (saṃskāra), there is no [male] of one's own lineage (svagotra). 187.

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and other ceremonies to be performed; thereafter, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products (*gavya*) and a ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), one should proceed.
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed,
even when impurity due to death has arisen, just as in the case of birth-impurity. (189)
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurity;
a woman in childbirth is purified by another who has given birth, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. (190)
If one travels for more than five days but less than ten days, the journey is considered completed after the tenth day;
if it occurs on the final day of the previous period, it is purified by two days, and if at dawn, by three days. (191)
From this point on, one should increase [the period] by one, two, or three days starting from half a day.
Listen now in due order to the impurity prescribed for the lowest artisans, beginning with the potter. (192)
One becomes pure after thirty-five days regarding the impurity caused by birth or death;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage should indeed perform the funeral rites.
If it is the daughter on the thirty-fifth day, then for those born under the Sahaja [Nakṣatra],
it would be the seventeenth day of the Yuga; on the thirteenth day, it is the fifth.
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after eleven days; in the seventh, it is ten days in succession.
This applies to those who have entered another *gotra* regarding both inheritance and impurity (*āśauca*). (195)
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that it applies to the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief. (196)
For a son who is given away by his parents, the prescribed period of impurity applies;
however, he does not share that impurity with his paternal kinsmen, according to the sequence of rules. || 197 ||
He who, having been given away by his parents in childhood to another, performs work there, is known as a *rūḍhahārī*; his sin is now described. (198)
There is no connection with the former lineage, nor ever with one's parents; for once the disciple has begun the rites, he becomes an attendant of the teacher. (199)
If impurity should arise for the sacrificer before the completion of the ritual act,
he should perform a bath with cow-products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, according to the sequence, it applies to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise to yogis. (201)

If at the time [of the birth] an impurity has arisen, one should observe that same period of impurity; this applies even if there is no one of one's own lineage (gotra) for the performance of the purificatory rites and other ceremonies. 202.

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; thereafter, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (*gavyasnāna*) and the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if it were the impurity of childbirth. (204)

Birth-impurity is purified by the death-impurity, and death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurity; one who has given birth is purified only by another birth-impurity, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. (205)
If one travels for more than five days but less than ten, the journey is completed after ten days;
if it occurs on the final day of the first period, one is purified by two days; if at dawn, by three days. (206)

From this point on, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, or three [units] starting from half a day. This is declared to be the "Low" (adhamā) stage of the potter; now hear about the "Royal" (rājakī) stages. || 207 ||
Whether it be impurity due to birth or impurity due to death, one becomes purified;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage should indeed perform the rite for the removal of sin. (208)
If it is a daughter on the thirty-sixth day, then for the Sahaja and Ātman [houses], there shall be a ten-day period of the Yugamūrti; [the remaining] four... [209]
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after six days; in the seventh, it is seven days, and so on for the Rudra days (eleven days), respectively.
This applies to those who have entered another gotra, regarding both inheritance and impurity.
"Therefore, there is impurity for the husband and for the wife as well; of this there is no doubt.
Or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief. (211)
For a son who is given away by his parents, the prescribed period of impurity applies;
however, he does not share that impurity with his paternal kinsmen, nor does it apply to them in succession.
If one who was given away by his parents to another during childhood performs work for that person, he shall be a *rutthahārī*; that [offense] is now described as *ādha*. (213)
(166) There is never any connection with one's former lineage or with one's parents; for once they have begun their practice as disciples, they become attendants of the Teacher. (214)
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the patron (yajamāna),
he should perform a bath with cow products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards, according to the sequence of the appropriate days;
and the same applies to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise to yogis.
If, at the time [of birth], that impurity has already arisen, one should observe it;
however, if there is no one of one's own lineage for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (saṃskāra), then [the following applies].

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (*gavyasnāna*) and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should undoubtedly cause all ritual acts to be performed;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if there were birth-impurity. (219)

Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for purifying death-impurity; one who has given birth is purified only by another birth-impurity, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. 220.
If one departs for ten days when it is slightly more than five days [remaining], the departure occurs after the tenth day;
if on the final day of the former period, there is purification after two days, then at dawn it is after three days.
From this point on, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, or three [units] starting from half a day.
This is declared to be the *rājakāgha*; now hear the *sūcikāgha*.
Impurity due to birth or impurity due to death is purified after thirty-six days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage shall indeed perform the rite for the removal of sin.
If it is the daughter on the thirty-sixth day, then for the Sahaja and Ātman [houses], there shall be the Daśāha period of Yugamūrti; on the fourteenth day, it is Pañcamī. (224)
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after six days; in the seventh, after eleven days, in due order.
This applies to those who have entered another lineage (gotra), regarding both inheritance and impurity (āśauca). || 225 ||
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that there is also impurity for the wife;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.
For that son who was given away by his parents, the period of impurity is prescribed; however, he did not have impurity with his paternal kinsmen, nor did it apply to them in due order. || 227 ||
If one who was given away by his parents to another during childhood performs work there, he shall be considered a *rutthahārī*; that sin is now being described.
p.
169) There is no connection with the former lineage, nor ever with the two parents; for once the rites have begun, the disciple indeed becomes an attendant of the teacher. || 229 ||
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the patron of the sacrifice,
he should perform a bath with cow-products and then carry out the remaining rites.
One should observe the period of impurity afterwards, according to the sequence of the appropriate days;
and the same applies to those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise to yogins.

If at the time [of birth] something has occurred, one should observe impurity accordingly; furthermore, if there is no one of one's own lineage for the rites of consecration and so forth, [one should act as follows].

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (*gavyasnāna*) and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should cause all ritual acts to be performed without any doubt;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if there were the impurity of childbirth. (234)
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurity;
one who has given birth is purified by another who has given birth, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. (235)
If the journey takes slightly more than five days—up to ten days—the departure is considered to have occurred after the tenth day.
If the departure occurs on the final day of the first period, one becomes pure after three days at dawn on the second day.
From this point on, one should increase [the period] by one, two, or three days starting from half a day.
This is declared to be the lowest grade of impurity for a needle-maker; now hear the impurity regarding the sale of oil. || 237 ||
Impurity due to birth or impurity due to death is purified after thirty-six days;
if a son is born within one's own lineage, those of that lineage should indeed perform the funeral rites.
If one desires [the result] on the thirty-sixth day, then there shall be the period (*daśā*) of Sahaja and Ātman for ten days;
and on the fourteenth day, the fifth [period] occurs. (239)
In the sixth generation, purification occurs after six days; in the seventh, it is seven days, and so on for eleven days respectively.
This applies to the inheritance and the period of impurity for those who have entered another *gotra*.
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that there is also impurity for the wife;
or else, I shall explain it in another way in brief.
For a son who is given away by his parents, the period of impurity is prescribed; however, he does not share that impurity with his paternal kinsmen in the same manner. || 242 ||
If one who was given away by his parents in childhood to another becomes a laborer there, he shall be the thief of that [stolen] wealth; likewise, the lowest [type of thief] is now described. (243)
p.
172) There is no connection with the previous lineage (gotra), nor ever with the two parents; for once the disciple has begun the rites, he becomes an attendant of the teacher. || 244 ||
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the sacrificer,
he should perform a bath with cow-products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.

One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, according to the sequence, one may perform the rite on a suitable day for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise for yogis. (246)

If, at the time when [an impurity] has arisen, one should observe that period of impurity; provided, however, that for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (saṃskāra), there is no one of one's own lineage (gotra). 247.
One should perform the purificatory rites and other such acts, and carry out those rituals;
afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products and a ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), [one should proceed].
Furthermore, one should perform all ritual duties without any doubt,
even when the impurity of death has arisen, just as one would during the impurity of childbirth. (249)

Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but death-impurity is not purified by birth-impurity; one who has given birth is purified by another who has given birth, and death-impurity is purified by death-impurity itself. (250)
If one travels for ten days when it is less than five days more [than the previous period], the journey ends after ten days;
if on the final day of the former period, then at dawn, purification occurs after two days, or after three days.
From this point on, one should increase [the period] by one, two, or three days starting from half a day.
Impurity is declared for the sale of oil; impurity is declared for the sale of betel-leaf. || 252 ||
Impurity due to birth and impurity due to death are both purified in thirty-six days. || 253 ||
If a son is born within one's own lineage, one should perform the rite of expiation (aghamaśrāddha) for that lineage.

If it is a daughter on the thirty-sixth day, then for those born under the Sahaja-nakṣatra, the period (daśā) of the twin-forms (Yugamūrti) shall last ten days; on the fourteenth day, it is the fifth [period]. (255)
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after six days; in the seventh, it is eleven days in succession.
This applies to those who have entered another lineage (gotra), regarding both inheritance and impurity.
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that it applies to the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief.
The impurity prescribed for that son who was given away by his parents is as follows:
his impurity was shared with his kinsmen, and it occurred according to the proper sequence. || 258 ||
If one who was given away by his parents in childhood to another becomes a laborer there, he shall be considered a *rutthahārī*; likewise, the *aghamarṣaṇa* is now described.
(175) There is no connection with a previous lineage, nor ever with one's parents; for once the rites have been commenced, the disciple becomes an attendant of the teacher. (260)
If impurity arises for the sacrificer before the completion of the rite,
he should then perform a bath with cow-products and proceed with the remainder of the ritual.

One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, according to the sequence, one should perform the rite on an appropriate day for those who have been initiated, for those established in vows, and likewise for yogins.

If, at the time [of birth], that impurity has already arisen, one should observe it; however, if there is no one of one's own lineage (gotra) for the rites such as the consecration (saṃskāra), then [the following applies].

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; thereafter, on an auspicious day, having performed the cow-urine bath (*gavyasnāna*) and the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should cause all ritual acts to be performed without any doubt,
just as it would be when impurity due to birth occurs during the impurity caused by death. (265)
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity is not purified by the rites for the dead;
one who has given birth is purified only by another who has given birth, and one affected by death-impurity is purified by another who has suffered a death.
If one travels for more than five days but less than ten, the journey is considered completed after ten days.
If it occurs on the final day of the first period, one becomes pure after two days; if at dawn, after three days. (267)
From this point on, one should increase [the dose] by one, two, or three [units] starting from half a day;
this is declared as the transformation of betel. Now hear about the lowliest Gopālas. || 268 ||
Impurity due to birth or impurity due to death is purified in one month; if a son is born within one's own lineage, that lineage is purified after three months. (269)
If [the rite] for a daughter is performed within one month, it is the same as for those born together;
that [rite] would be on the fifteenth day, and on the eleventh day, it is the fifth.
In the sixth [generation], purification occurs after nine days; in the seventh, after eight days, respectively.
This applies to those who have entered another lineage (gotra) regarding both inheritance and impurity (āśauca). || 271 ||
If there is impurity for the husband, there is no doubt that it applies to the wife as well;
or else, I shall explain it in another way, in brief.
The impurity prescribed for a son who is given away by his parents is as follows:
however, there was no impurity for him to observe in due order along with his paternal kinsmen.
One who, having been given away by his parents in childhood to another, performs labor there, shall be a *rutthahārī*; now, the *aghamarṣaṇa* is being described.
There is never any connection with one's former lineage or with one's parents; for once a disciple has begun the rites, he becomes an attendant of his teacher. (275)
If impurity arises before the completion of the ritual for the sacrificer,
he should perform a bath with cow-products and then carry out the remainder of the rite.

One should observe the period of impurity afterwards; then, according to the sequence, one should choose a suitable day for those who have been initiated, those established in vows, and likewise for yogins. (277)

If, at the time [of birth], that impurity has already arisen, one should observe it; provided, however, that for the rites such as the consecratory ceremonies (saṃskāra), there is no other person of one's own lineage (gotra). 278.

One should cause the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to be performed and carry out those rituals; afterwards, on an auspicious day, having performed a bath with cow-products (*gavya*) and a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, one should cause all ritual actions to be performed without doubt;
even when impurity due to death has arisen, it should be as if it were the impurity of childbirth. (280)
Childbirth is purified by [the period of] death, but death is not purified by the rites for childbirth;
one who has given birth is purified only by the period of childbirth, and one who has died is purified by the period of death. (281)
If one travels for more than five days but less than ten, the journey [is considered complete] after ten days.
If [the journey] begins on the last day of the previous period, one is purified after two days; if it begins at dawn, after three days. (282)
From this point, starting from half a day, one should increase [the duration] by one, two, or three [days] in sequence.
This is declared to be the "cowherd sin" (gopālāgha); now listen to the specific sins (viśeṣāgha). || 283 ||

For one who has been initiated, for a man with an only son, and when his mother or father has died, there is indeed no impurity (sūtaka) or impurity due to death (pretaka) regarding festivals and other rites up until the pilgrimage site. 284.
One should perform the consecration in the sacrificial hall and carry out the remnants of the sacrifice; however, for his son there is a special rule: he becomes pure immediately by bathing. (285)
For those who have been initiated, those established in vows, ascetics, and celibate students, neither impurity due to birth nor impurity due to death ever exists. (286)
Neither physical transformation nor advanced age makes one unfit for celibacy;
having abandoned this scripture, one should not contemplate another scripture. (287)
If the teachers [of the ritual] are present before the arising of sin—from the commencement of the rites until their completion—it is declared that they are faultless. (288)
If their forms existed previously, it is said that there is no fault arising from sin when an action is undertaken and completed. (289)
If their agents existed previously, it is said that [the act] is faultless; yet, from the commencement of the action until its completion, there arises the production of demerit (adharma). (290)
If it is argued that their past actions are faultless because sin arises only from the commencement of an action until its completion, [then this is not so]. (291)
This is declared to be a particularly grave offense; now hear the rule for expiation.
One should cause the fault that has arisen at the time of commencing the rite to be remedied. (292)
Indeed, a rite filled with defects leads to harm; one should offer the oblation for the crow-like tongue.
Furthermore, they perform the rites for the gods using products of the cow. (293)
The most excellent preceptor should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma);
thereafter, he should cause pure food to be given, accompanied by pure food.
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and filled with the clamor of musical instruments,
they, indeed, through delusion, engaged in battle itself. (295)
The most excellent preceptor should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and the fire-oblation to the image (mūrtihoma);
thereafter, he should cause pure food accompanied by clarified butter (śuddhasamanvita) to be offered. || 296 ||
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and filled with the resonance of musical instruments,
[the ritual proceeds] starting from the circular pedestal (pīṭha) all the way to the interior of the sanctum (garbhageha).
Furthermore, regarding the touching [of the disciple], specific rites have been illustrated;
such as the removal of the funeral pyre (aśmodvāsana) or causing [the deity] to enter [the disciple] by means of dūrvā grass, and so forth. || 298 ||
One should perform the ceremonial bathing at the aforementioned locations and ensure it does not touch the image;
thereafter, one should cause pure food to be offered, accompanied by pure food. (299)

If one who knows the mantras should cause [the rite] to be performed accompanied by the sound of conchs, filled with the noise of musical instruments, and associated with the materials required for impurity, (p. 183) [then it is so]. 300.
Then, after performing the bathing of the deities for worship and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma),
one should subsequently cause pure food to be given, accompanied by pure food.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs and filled with the noise of musical instruments—this is declared to be the rule for impurity, as spoken in all the scriptures. (302)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the rules on impurity, in the Candrajñāna.
p. 184) Śrī (The Chapter on the Great Festival)
I shall describe the procedure for the great festival; listen with a one-pointed mind.
It is for the sake of increasing the prosperity of the entire kingdom and for ever augmenting victory. (1)
For the purpose of destroying all diseases and bringing about the pleasure of all people,
first comes the offering of the flag-sprout (dhvajāṅkurārpaṇa), and second, the festival-sprout (utsavāṅkura).
The third is the sprout of the sacred site (tīrthāṅkura), which is threefold and concludes with the festival;
the first is the sacrifice of the bull (vṛṣayāga), and the second is the seat of the deity (devatāsana).
The third should be the sound of the drum, the fourth the offering of oblations (bali),
the fifth the ascent (rohaṇa), and the sixth the sacrificial hall (yāgaśālaka).
One should perform the seventh rite of curiosity (kautuka), the eighth in the ritual of fire-oblation (homa),
the ninth one should perform as a festival (utsava), and the tenth as the enclosure (pariveṣṭaka).
p.
185) It is said that for Gaṇapati, the ritual bath itself constitutes the wearing of the marriage-thread (*kautuka*).
Having performed the circumambulation of the village, [one should offer] a cake and a plantain fruit. (6)
The eleventh is the mounting of the chariot, the twelfth is the descent;
the thirteenth is the [offering of] unguents, and the fourteenth is the powder festival.
At the commencement of the rite and at its conclusion, one should perform the sixteen-fold Caṇḍayāga;
thereafter follows the lowering of the banner, and after that, the pure ablution.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the Gaurī-yāga, followed immediately by the festival for the devotees;
having understood this which is known as the twentyfold division, one should carry out the ritual action.
The festival is to be known as threefold: Puṣkala, Vijaya, and Paitra;
the latter lasts for twelve days, while the tenth belongs to Śiva.
(186) But preceded by the hoisting of the banner, the rite of the sprouts is performed, preceded by the drum. || 11 ||
On that day, preceded by the ritual planting of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
the preeminent preceptor should commence the raising of the flagstaff (dhvaja) at either three or two times the [usual] duration.
One should begin the festival for the installation at the time of Pradoṣa;
the rising [of the image] should take place in the forenoon, at midday, or in the afternoon.
On that day, or even for a mere moment, the wise man should sow [the seed] in this manner:
in the forenoon for the class of Brahmins, and at midday for [the other classes].

In the evening, for the sake of all protection, that which always increases victory—from the raising of the banner up to the end of the ritual at the sacred ford—is called the "Complete" (Sākalya) rite. || 15 ||
Except for Mars, which belongs to Śiva (the bull-bannered one), the remaining [planets] belong to the ancient deities as previously stated;
this is declared to be the conclusion of the sowing [of seeds], being pacified according to their respective desires. (16)
Some, through devotion, perform the festival of Śiva at the [proper] time... Thus, the peaceful [rite] has been fully described; now the auspicious rite is likewise being told. (17)
Whether in the forenoon or the afternoon, when a festival is performed exclusively [for this purpose], it is declared to be auspicious; thus [it is said] three times... || 18 ||
One should then perform the festival during these four types of months: the solar, the civil (sāvana), the lunar, and the lunar-asterismal (nakṣatra). || 19 ||
Up to the Saura and Sāvana tīrthas, the fruit shall be residence in the same world (sālokya) and so forth;
up to the Candranakṣatra tīrtha, it brings all prosperity and happiness.

O Lord, one should place the deity upon that very sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), which corresponds to the solar zodiac sign where the sun is situated, using the hand itself; likewise, three [handfuls] should be offered. (21)
Thereafter, having tied the *pratisara* with the *tryambaka* mantra itself,
the binding of the *pratisara* should indeed be performed on the right hand of the deities.
With the mantra "bṛhatsāma," the wise one should likewise provide a protective amulet for the goddess; with the mantra "mantravāsa," he should give her the incense of consecrated substances.
The Venerable One should cause it to be proclaimed with five mantras by the assembly of Brahmans;
he should offer unbroken grains to the deity and cause incense and lamps to be presented.
Mudga-rice, taḍḍuka, and various kinds of cakes for eating, combined with all types of side-dishes, along with clarified butter mixed with milk. (25)
Then one should present the oblation with the mantra "madhuvātā ṛtāyate";
thereafter, having discarded the remains of the offering (*nirmālya*), [one should perform the subsequent rites]. (p. 189) || 26 ||
Afterwards, having offered betel-leaf, he should show a mirror;
then the wise man should cause an umbrella and a chowrie to be presented.
One should show the Brahmins [the image] with the mantra "brahmajajñānam";
with the mantra "gaur dhenuḥ bhavyā," one should show the cow together with her calf and limbs.
Having bound the *pratisara* of Nandīśa, one should strike the great musical instrument;
having summoned all the musicians, one should display them at the great festival (*mahānāḍī*).
And he was purified by that very [performance] which was joined with song and accompanied by dancers.
One should cause the islands to be placed upon a palanquin adorned with all ornaments;
having circumambulated the palace, one should enter the pavilion of the assembly hall. (31)
Accompanied by dance, song, and other such performances, there shall indeed be a vigil at night;
and at the clear dawn, the preceptor should perform his ritual bath.

Having adorned him with a turban and an upper garment, anointed him with all kinds of fragrant unguents, and decorated him with all ornaments, one should likewise embellish him with every kind of garland.
Having covered Naṭeśvara with a cloth and endowed him with all ornaments,
one should prepare two altars and place the image on one of them.
On the second day, one should place a covering over the funeral pyre using black fragrant substances;
having divided the fragrance into three parts upon that, one should then have the *pūṇyāha* rite recited.
One should perform the vow for the sake of purifying the fragrance while facing the deity;
moreover, the wise one should especially perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya) by means of oblations (homa). (36)
For the purpose of purifying the fragrance, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, and cooked rice with the mantra "Gandhadvārām. (37)
And likewise, one should perform that which is appropriate for the vow with forest-grown roots and mantras,
using clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), as well as sesame, mung beans, and barley.
The wise one should offer oblations of parched grain, a hundred for each;
having performed this special fire-sacrifice, the intelligent preceptor likewise [proceeds]. (39)

Having spoken only of the pervasion of the *homa*, and not having given a cow, those who do not perform [the rite] have stated only the month and the lunar mansion; for it has indeed been said thus, and in this very way.
Having determined the month and the lunar day for each year, conjoined with the [appropriate] asterism.
One should undertake the commencement during a festival or at any time of one's choosing within the month;
it shall be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. || 42 ||
However, prior to the commencement of the sacrifice, if a kinsman is present, there is a reversal [of the order]. || 43 ||
An expiation must indeed be performed; one should carry out a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) until the end of Ārdrā, or until the end of Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), or likewise until Rohiṇī.
Regarding the question of what must be performed in all months according to the Smṛti, [it is said]:
"By means of the procedure prescribed for a single month, [the rite] is to be performed... (p. 193) || 146 ||
At the time for the commencement of the festival of Śiva, another festival was not desired;
yet, at the time for the festival of another deity, the festival of Mahādeva was performed. || 48 ||
Those festivals of the gods that were commenced previously incur no fault;
however, one that is commenced in the midst of Śiva’s festival incurs all faults. (49)
If one performs both the Śiva-sacrifice and another sacrifice at the same time,
one obtains that [latter] in vain, for it cannot be performed upon a single substance.
One should not employ a bannerless banner; rather, one should employ the bull-bannered [Śiva].
Even for the welfare of the gods, one should not cause a human-like banner to be made. (51)
If one should cause grief to be done, one will incur the sorrow of disease,
whether in a village, a city, a town, or a capital.
One should perform a festival for all the gods; no fault is found in this.
A wise person should cause the commencement of the festival to be performed in three ways. || 53 ||
One should begin the hoisting of the flag during the twenty-seventh lunar mansion;
for twenty-eight days, however, the beating of the drum shall be as before.
Now listen to the immediate consecration (adhivāsana) preceded by the offering of the sprouts;
however, following the hoisting of the banner, one should subsequently strike the drum.
First there should be the proclamation by the sounding of the drum, and afterwards the ascent;
first there should be the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkura), and afterwards one should strike the drum. (56)
This day, in brief, is thus on the first day;
one should perform the immediate consecration (adhivāsana) throughout that entire day.
One should fashion the characteristics of the banner-cloth (dhvajapaṭa) as twelve cubits, or likewise ten cubits, or even seven cubits. || 58 ||
The śikhara (spire) should be known as having six, five, or even four tālas; it is provided with three tails and joined with two additional tails. (59)
Having divided that seat into five parts, O Vṛṣapālikā,
the central part is joined with a white lotus seat, whether it be standing or reclining.
If one draws [the deity] white in color, smoky, red, or even black in color, the king and his kingdom will perish. (61)
By means of a white-colored bull, one should cause the kingdom and the king to prosper;
it brings about all peace, is meritorious, and bestows happiness upon the entire world.
The body should be white in color; the two forelegs of the illustrious cow should be red, the two ears yellow, and one should draw the tail in that same color.
The eye should be painted black, white, and likewise blue;
from the tips of the feet, one should extend the color red and the color blue.
On the sides, however, a lamp alone is prescribed; the wise one should have it fashioned like a trident, as well as an umbrella, two chowries, and a svastika facing upwards. (65)
One should then draw the incense and the bell; the wise one should likewise depict the lamp, the sprout, and the full vase adorned with flowers. (66)
Adorned with all ornaments, it is the cause of the knowledge of Śiva; the second [rite] is the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga), which brings about liberation through the application of the means.
In front of the deity, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with eight droṇas of śāli rice;
