having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, fashion the pericarp in its center.
In the middle [altar],
having established the Bull (Vṛṣabha) and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) in the jars,
one should worship the World-Protectors with their respective personal mantras. || 70 ||

The wise one should worship with the seed-syllable of Vṛṣa and with perfumes and other offerings; he should also perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice, as well as with the specific substances.

One should offer oblations in sequence with the *jayā* and other mantras, with the *abhaya*, the *dhāna*, and the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* mantras; then, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti* while holding the pitcher upon one's head. || 72 ||
Thus he [recites] the mantra...
and Trimūrti...
at that time, one should offer incense, a lamp, and an oblation of food.
The bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga) has been fully described, and then the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) in due order;
having worshipped the second [deity], the third shall be the invocation (āvāhana).
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there; the *kautuka* [should be placed] in the middle of the trident.
On the root of the leaf of the three-leaved [tree], one should place the Trimūrti, and on the root of the leaf of the three-petalled [tree], the Triśaktikā. (76)
Pālikā, Guhameva, [and] Kamtatra, as well as Meva; likewise Caṇḍeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and Bhāskara. || 77 ||
Mahāśāstṛ, Mahākālī, and likewise Mahāmodī; those seven Mothers, as well as Vighneśa and Vīrabhadra. (78)
A wise person, for the sake of pleasing all the gods, should cause the feet of the Vidyeśvaras to be made at the base of the staff, and the earth in the form of a trident. (79)
Having worshipped according to the rules with perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, water for honor, and water for the feet— this is the third [stage]— the fourth is the beating of the drum.
A *paṭaha* drum should be seven *tālas* in length, while a *bherī* drum should be five *tālas*.
A drum of four *tālas* is declared to be of medium size, and one of three *tālas* shall be considered inferior. (81)
One should take the Samada, Carṇaka, and Devadāru trees at the edge of the Uśīra forest; such shall be the characteristics of the Bherikā drum.
Having worshipped Rudra on the right, one should worship Viṣṇu on the left;
in the middle, Prajāpati, and at his strike, Skanda himself.
Vāsukī is also [the deity] for the thread, and indeed Candramas for the bracelet;
Jayakhaṇḍī is the deity for the ritual action, and Rudraka as well.
Vaśya has Tamburu as its deity, and Nārada is likewise [the deity] of the lute;
Śaṅkha has the Moon and Sword as its deities, and Diti is the deity of the timila drum.
The preceptor, having invoked the deities presiding over all the musical instruments as well as the flower,
and having summoned the instrumentalist, shall be well-bathed and clad in pure garments. (86)
One who has been initiated, who is pure, supreme, and auspicious—such a woman one should choose; however, one should avoid those of other castes.
One should also avoid one who is diseased, one who is deficient in limb, and one who lacks spiritual power. || 87 ||
Endowed with all auspicious marks and for the sake of bestowing all prosperity,
one should offer incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra and then bind the protective thread (kautuka) in due order.
In this manner, one should worship the sacred thread, the upper garment, and the cloth;
likewise, one should worship all the musical instruments and the drum itself.
The procedure for the seven palm-tree measures has been declared; both the teacher and the disciple, accompanied by the sounding of kettledrums, should worship the deities of the joints.
At the time of playing the instruments, one should worship the trident and the food-liṅga;
then, with the mantra "brahmajajñānam," one should first strike [the drum] with the Ghora [mantra]. (91)
The wise one should strike it a second time with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇu," and likewise the third watch with the mantra "tryambaka."
The musician, with flowers in hand, having offered salutations and praise to the drum (bherī), [performs] the ritual of the seven beats; this has been declared for both the teacher and the disciple.
One should worship the deities of the junctions accompanied by the sound of a drum;
likewise, one should offer a trident, a food-liṅga, and a vessel for the sacrificial oblation.
Having performed the circumambulation of the village, one should worship the deities of the junctions, as well as the one whose banner is the bull and the moon-crested Lord Śiva himself.
One should worship a bull there; a flagstaff is prescribed [to be made of] *campaka*, *candana*, *kramuka*, or a bamboo staff. (96)
One should avoid the *bilva*, the *devadāru*, the *akana*, and likewise the *khadira* trees; one should also avoid those that are crooked, split, hollow, or contain worm-holes.
The height of the chariot (vimāna) is prescribed for the flagstaff;
it should extend from the chest level, or up to the end of the neck (gulānta), or even up to the pinnacle (stūpyanta). || 98 ||
It may be equal to three tālas, or equal to the gopura, or equal to one tāla, or specifically up to the pinnacle (sthūpī). || 99 ||
One should first perform the Śiva-festival for a temple that lacks a celestial chariot (vimāna),
and having carried out the restoration of what is dilapidated, one should perform the Śiva-sacrifice.
The height of the staff is prescribed as twenty-one [units] in conjunction [with the other measurements]. || 101 ||
Indeed, the *daṇḍotsedha* celestial chariot is prescribed as the location for the banner;
it should be placed either in the middle of the pedestal at the gate-tower (*gopura*), or at the front of the pedestal, or at the tip of the bull.
Either at the beginning or in the middle of the Mahāmāyī [mandala], the location for the banner (dhvaja) is prescribed;
one should then dig the earth to a depth and width of two cubits.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains and place a golden brush (kūrca) upon it;
its size should be six tālas, five tālas, or nine tālas for the most excellent [mandala].
In brief, the length of the flagstaff, including its extension, is threefold; having made it equal to that [length], its form should be shaped like a bow.
It should be provided with two hollows, or even just one half-hollow; furthermore,
there should be three joints at the tip of the staff, each at an equal interval of three units.
A wise person should have it made eight finger-breadths in circumference, like a cord;
the ring, or "cord-ring," is double [that] and rests upon the base.
Having spread the garland of *darbha* grass, listen to the characteristics of the altar:
its width should be two cubits and its height one cubit.
Equipped with three girdles, each mountain [should be] one finger-breadth [in height];
the wise one, skilled in ritual procedures, should fashion a pericarp in the middle.
Or, one may place [the lotus] joined with a single girdle in the center of the pericarp;
it should be red, equal to the secondary altar (upavedī), three finger-breadths in width, and equal to that [in height]. || 110 ||
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, one should then dismiss the artisan;
perform the sprinkling with pure water mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (111)
At the base of the staff is the principle of Brahmā (brahmatattva), in the middle is the principle of Viṣṇu (viṣṇutattva),
at the tip is the principle of Rudra (rudratattva), and on the cloth is the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
The wise one should thus arrange the staff for the gods on the left;
having first established the water-pot in the east, he should perform the consecration at the base of the staff.
One should establish the guardians of the quarters with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra and their own respective mantras;
likewise, one should perform dance, song, and instrumental music.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, one should present everything up to the food offering (naivedya), including my favorite food,
sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), and all varieties of plantain fruit.
One should fashion a ball [of clay] the size of a wood-apple fruit, and ten more of the same;
if it is surrounded by auspicious [deities], one should then have it performed as if for a son. (116)
One should never perform [the rite] for inauspicious maidens;
rather, one should then worship the sixfold [deity] accompanied by all sounds.
The seventh sacrificial hall is prescribed as the sacrificial hall;
it should have either sixteen pillars or thirty-two pillars.
Then, one should have a pavilion constructed provided with four pillars;
having established the altar in the center, the wise one should then designate the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). || 119 ||

The nine-fire rite is declared for the best [practitioner], the five-fire rite should be for the middling, and one should know that the single-fire rite is for the lowest; thus should the wise man arrange them.
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, carry out the circumambulation with fire;
then, having wound a garland of *darbha* grass, let it be beautified above the canopy. (121)
One should fashion it with yoke-poles and arches in the four directions;
likewise, one should worship the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala) outside the altar.
A conch shell, a lamp, likewise a svastika, two chowries, a bull, a full water-pot, a mirror, and likewise Lakṣmī. (123)
One should worship the deity holding the ten weapons outside the water-pot (kumbha);
the Śiva-kumbha in the center, and the Vardhanī to its north.
Having worshipped the eight jars on all sides, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas);
one should then worship the door-jars provided at the four doors.
Having established the water-pot (kumbha) in the northeast, surrounded by the eight Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvara),
one should worship the pot at that door which faces the direction of the entrance of the *liṅga*. (126)
Having conceived the site as before, one should then worship the doors and so forth;
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
One should worship Nivṛtti in the east, and likewise Pratiṣṭhā in the south;
one should worship Vidyā in the west, and Śānti in the north.
Having worshipped the door-arches, one should worship the four Vedas;
likewise, the altar, the form of the altar, the secondary altar, and the seal-ring.
The weapon is sacred to all the deities; at Maṅgala, one should worship the eight beautiful goddesses.
There, one should worship Yāgeśa and sacrifice to Umāskandeśvara.
Having stood well-positioned in front of the pavilion, one should then bind the *kautuka* (protective thread),
specifically with a gold thread or otherwise with cotton thread. (131)
One should place a bundle of ashes wrapped in a new cloth,
held in the hand of an attendant, while circumambulating the enclosure wall from left to right.
Then, when the presence of the deity has been attained, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana);
subsequently, with the excellent mantra "Tryambakaṃ," the binding of the protective thread (rakṣāsūtra) is performed.
One should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) provided with incense and lamps;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there, and thereafter feed the devotees.
There, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented and properly provide betel-leaf;
beginning with the beating of the kettledrum, this is done during the collection of the offering in the village.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should establish Umāskandeśvara;
at its end is the Dīpa-yāntra, and at the end of that is the Ḍolā-yāntra. (136)
After that, there was a horse-chariot, then a womb-chariot, and a chariot for men, all equipped with various lamps and accompanied by various devotees. (137)
It was equipped with various banners and adorned with various parasols;
it resounded with conchs and trumpets, and was filled with the booming of kettledrums. || 138 ||
Having written them down, they should proceed immediately with those ending in mechanical devices;
then, in the next [section], there are mechanical horses, mechanical musical instruments, and mechanical dancing.
Or one should arrange a flood on the northern bank of a river;
and at its extremities, one should provide food for the Brāhmaṇas immediately thereafter.
On the other side of the kings, within the proximity of men of knowledge;
on the other side of the Rudras, having gone into the midst of heretics. (141)
With the great army of meditative concentrations, one should swiftly cast forth the offering substances:
sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, as well as incense and lamps. (142)
Having placed water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) in their respective vessels,
one should daily deposit the materials for the bali-offering into the bali-vessel.
On the first day, according to the ritual procedure, one should offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), mung-bean rice, molasses with parched grain flour, and sesame seeds.
One should daily offer oblations to the world-protectors (lokapālas) by their respective names in due order:
at night, a full lotus and milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds.
And on the second day, recollecting the Brahma-mantra,
[he offered] beloved items, ghee, rice mixed with flour, and likewise [other offerings].
On the third day, while recollecting the mantra of the Bhūtas,
one should offer at night a coconut, ghee, rice, and likewise Sarala wood.
And on the fourth day, recollecting the Gandharva, [one should offer] mixed with priyaṅgu and ghee... || 148 ||
Water for drinking, mouth-freshener, betel-leaf, and likewise the hand itself. (149)
There, the preceptor should cause [the offering] to be given; he should cause it to be given with the right hand. Provided with the right foot, one becomes a female attendant of Rudra. || 150 ||
Adorned with every ornament, [he was] equipped with all [attire] for the age; [this was] for the sake of the hunting expedition... || 151 ||
At the base, one should bind the trident and likewise the image; having done so, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 152 ||
One should worship with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, half that amount of *taṇḍula* rice, and sesame seeds, along with gold, a *kūrca* of grass, and cloth, using perfumes and flowers.
Having bathed with pure water alone, according to the mantra, using the principal seed-syllable, [one should apply] the three fragrances in the three [vessels]... || 154 ||
On another day, at night, one should worship the root-liṅga;
having consecrated the water-jars and the fire in the sacrificial pit, one should offer perfumes and other articles in the prescribed order as before.
Then the preceptor should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the remaining materials;
thereafter, having dismissed the form of the fire, he should worship the guardians of the sacrificial image.
Having circumambulated the Lord of Sacrifice, the King of Śāstras, and the temple,
one should enter the inner sanctum and place [the deity] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
After performing the purification of the *liṅga* [and so forth],
one should then worship the Lord of Sacrifice, the *liṅga*, upon the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) together with the *vardhanī*.
One should place eight jars of satisfaction at the tips of the petals;
then one should perform the ritual bathing with one hundred and eight [vessels]. (159)
Having offered abundant oblations, one should present betel-leaf;
at night, one should worship Caṇḍeśa while reciting the Caṇḍagāyatrī.
One should especially perform the ceremonial bathing with nine jars;
likewise, one should perform the fire-oblation before Caṇḍa using the Caṇḍagāyatrī mantra.
One should worship Vṛṣadeva with the mantra "vṛṣasya tu vṛṣāya" at the base of the banner, honoring him with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the deities of the site (vāstudevas) exactly as before;
one should dismiss them in due order within each respective part of the site. 163.
Afterwards, one should worship Caṇḍeśa and offer sacrificial oblation;
and on the following day, one should worship the primary liṅga. || 164 ||
Having thus commenced the daily worship, one should observe silence and perform the hand-worship;
at its conclusion, one should perform the ritual bathing, followed immediately by the pure bath.
Then one should perform the great oblation (*mahāhavis*);
furthermore, one should especially honor the devotees and the attendants.
Just as a king would honor everyone according to the extent of his wealth, || 167 ||
Thereafter, one should cause the festival known as Śivotsava to be performed every year;
it increases longevity, prosperity, sons, grandsons, and all [other blessings]. (168)
The king attains everything beneficial for the kingdom, bringing about both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and achieves union with Śiva through the power of the festival of Śiva. || 169 ||
Thus ends the chapter on the ritual for the Great Festival in the *Devīmata*, according to the *Candrajñānabheda*.
Hariḥ oṃ.
For one who possesses the *Śrīkāmika*, daily libations (*tarpaṇa*) and offerings (*bali*) need not be performed.
On the very day the cremation ends, and for three days beginning with that of Īśa, [one should observe the vow]. || 1 ||

One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with half of that amount, and worship Śiva with half of that; [this is from] the Jñānaratnāvalī. Now, the *ānaṃda* (bliss) is being described in detail. || 2 ||
In this regard, for that yogi who has attained departure (utkrānti) and is free from all impurity,
one should burn his pure body, which consists of mantra, with the fire of Śiva.
Neither the rite of offering funeral cakes nor the rite of water libations should be performed;
rather, at that time, the disciples must perform the worship of Śiva for the sake of becoming free from their debt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the exposition of the knowledge of reality. (5)
The sequence of emanation, withdrawal, maintenance, this supreme differentiation,
and the vision of the states— this is called the fivefold objective reality. (6)
The differentiation of the thirty-six principles is known as the bondage of the individual soul (paśu-pāśa);
through the knowledge of the Lord (pati-jñāna), there shall likewise be union (sāyujya) and the attainment of the Self (ātma-lābha).
Thus, these ten divisions are indeed described in their proper sequence:
the Parāpara, the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), and the Nāda produced from Kuṭilā.
From Nāda, Bindu is produced; from Bindu, Sadāśiva arises;
from Sadāśiva, Īśa arises; and from that, Śuddhavidyā is born.
Arising from the primordial point (pūrvabindu), it is subtle and extends to the end of Vaikharī;
from that, the phonemes of Vaikharī are produced, and from those phonemes, the mantras arise.
From that, the web of scriptures arose through seventy million great mantras;
within the sounds, reality, emanation, and pure reality increase. (11)
Then, by the grace of Anantadeva, those born of Māyā arose:
Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, Vidyā, and Rāga. (12)
From Rudradeva was born Prakṛti, arising from the three guṇas;
and from that unmanifest Prakṛti arose the emergence of the mind (citta) and the intellect (buddhi). || 13 ||
When the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises from the intellect (buddhi), it becomes threefold; it is called by the three names: Taijasa, Vaikṛta, and Bhūtādi. || 14 ||
The Taijasa [ego] possesses the Sattva quality; from it arises the mind (manas). From the Jñānendriyas arises the Vaikharī [speech], and from the Karmendriyas arises the Ahaṃkāra. || 15 ||
From the tamasic ego (ahaṃkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra) arise;
from sound, space (ākāśa) is produced, and likewise, wind (vāyu) is said to have arisen from touch. (16)
In form (rūpa), fire is produced from the quality of passion (rajas); in taste, water arises;
and in smell, earth is produced—such is the activity of the effects of the principles (tattva-kārya). || 17 ||
Again, through the bond of the principles (tattvas), one should separate the earth from smell;
water from the bonds of taste; and one should properly join fire with form. || 18 ||
In the case of touch, one should bind the wind mixed with space for the sake of the perfection of sound;
from sound and so forth, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), and in the case of form, the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 19 ||
These five are the organs of action when the Rajas quality is joined with Vaikharī;
and these five are the organs of knowledge when the ego-sense has entered the Taijasa state.
The *bhūtādi* and the *vaikharī*, as well as the *taijasa* joined with *buddhi* and *citta*,
and those joined with *citta* and the *kṣetrajña*— these constitute the twenty-five *rāgas*. (21)
One should bind passion, ignorance, limited agency, necessity, and time within the principles (tattvas);
and one should apply the web of scriptures and the mantras within the mantra, and the mantra within the phonemes (varṇas). || 22 ||
The phonemes are joined with Vaikharī; Vaikharī is joined with Madhyamā;
Madhyamā indeed perceives Paśyantī; one should join Paśyantī with the Subtle (Sūkṣmā). || 23 ||
One should properly join the four subtle forms of speech to the initial bindu;
thereafter, one should join the [principles] from Śuddhavidyā up to Śiva within the curved [line].
One who is united with the supreme Śakti in the Supreme [Brahman] should join the principles (tattvas) together;
this has been declared as the sequence of creation and dissolution, and now the sequence of maintenance (sthitikrama) is being described.
Paraśiva has become transcendent; [His power] consisting of will, knowledge, and action—due to the rotation like a wheel of the fire situated in the previous karma... (p. 226) ...[is manifested]. 26.

The five elements beginning with space, the sense organs such as hearing presided over [by the deities], and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) such as sound, exist in the proximity of the Abode (dhāman). 27.
The five organs of action, beginning with speech, consist of speaking and so forth;
and the mind, intellect, ego, and the fourth, which is the consciousness (citta). || 28 ||

They know that ascertainment, the desire for [the goal], reflection, and the performance of action constitute what is celebrated as the reality of the self (ātmatattva); now hear from me concerning the vision (darśana) that follows.
The reality of time proceeds as the past, the present, and the future; destiny (niyati) brings about certainty by drawing forth the creative powers (kalās) born of action;
and knowledge (vidyā) consists of wisdom and the like. || 30 ||
The five [factors], beginning with the object (*viṣaya*), are active, while the Puruṣa remains the witness.
Māyā produces delusion in the mind; this is remembered as the *Ga-kāṇḍa*. (31)
An abundance of knowledge with a deficiency in action is the principle of Śuddhavidyā;
an abundance of action with subtlety of knowledge is known as the principle of Īśvara. || 32 ||
The principle of Śakti arises from action; the principle of Śiva is superior to that. || 33 ||
The Preraka-kāṇḍa—these five are remembered as the Śiva-tattva;
along with the gross, the subtle, and the supreme, this is the vision of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
One should demonstrate within the mouth of the Guru the supreme Śivatattva, which consists of Māyā and the other principles up to Satya, and which exists in a subtle form. || 35 ||
Within the ninety-six principles (*tattva*), it perpetually revolves like a wheel;
and that self, finding rest therein, gives rise to the activities of the five states. (36)

One should perform the fivefold [meditation] as "space" (vyoman) in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, extending from the forehead to the throat, the heart, the navel, and ending at the genitals. (37)
And the five states exist in the lower portion; hear now [about them]. The pentad beginning with the ear and the pentad beginning with sound likewise come into being. (38)

The five principles beginning with speech, the fivefold functions beginning with speaking, the ten vital airs beginning with prāṇa, and the fivefold group beginning with the mind, joined with the Puruṣas—[these constitute the thirty-six categories]. (39)
Thirty-five [channels] exist in the forehead, the locus of waking;
they consist of the ten [senses], beginning with sound, together with the vital breaths, such as prāṇa and the rest. (40)
The instrument (karaṇa), the fourth [state], and the twenty-five thorns; the enjoyment of objects while awake, as well as latent impressions (vāsanā) and the very act of bathing. (41)
Just as fire is kindled when iron and fire meet, and as wind [is stirred] by fire,
so too the mind and the vital breath, being joined within the field, indeed enter into deep sleep in the heart.
It manifests dream and the state of forgetfulness upon waking, as well as deep sleep;
it maintains the vital breath of the self, which resides at the root of the navel.
When there is no dreaming, no hearing, and the absence of the fourth state (turya), one is liberated;
at the root of the *liṅga*, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) attains that which is called "beyond the fourth" (*turyātīta*).
It may be gross, subtle, very subtle, or even more subtle than that;
the minister, possessing a fourfold army, has entered the innermost part of the king. (45)
(230) Thus, O King, the individual self (*jīvātman*) flows through five states;
now listen to the intermediate state following these. (46)
At the forehead, which is the locus of the waking state, one should show the ends of the past;
then, having understood both the lower and the middle states, the wise man proceeds thus.

These five pure principles are known as the supreme states (parasaṃsthā), occurring respectively in groups of four, three, two, and one; one should meditate upon them as being the waking state and the others.
Thus, the fifteen states and the three states are combined; [therein lie] the Kevala, the Sakala, and the Śuddha. Now, listen to the description of Darśana.
The states beginning with the waking state and ending with the fourth (turya) are known as Sakala;
that which transcends them is Kevala, which is remembered as being pure and joined with Smara.
The lower part, the middle, and the upper part constitute the threefold [state]; this is called the state of *māyā*. Now hear concerning that which is perceived in the waking state. (51)
The fourfold group beginning with Śiva, the group beginning with Kalā, and the group beginning with Manas;
the sense organs beginning with hearing, the single principle [of ego], and the objects of sense such as sound joined with the one [principle]. (52)
In the waking states, the reality is seen as associated with the eighteen [tattvas];
however, through the mere presence of Śiva, the Self always abides [in its true nature]. (53)
Through the application of yoga and nyāsa, the wise man perceives [the self] within the states of waking;
the engagement with objects of perception in the waking state is stilled by pratyāhāra. (54)
One should conquer sleep through *dhāraṇā*, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) indeed through *dhyāna*,
the fourth state (*turya*) through *samādhi*, and that which transcends the fourth (*turyātīta*) through Śiva.
By the instruction of the true guru, through its own self-luminosity, [the mind becomes] immovable;
thus is described the fivefold meaning of the stainless state. (56)
Impurity, karma, māyā, mahāmāyā, and that which conceals—these alone are said to be the five objects; now hear the definition of direct perception. || 57 ||
The nature of will, knowledge, and action is not perceived apart from the awakening of the Self;
having rendered it like copper and black iron, it is called the individual power (āṇava-śakti). 58.

The threefold forms—namely, that which has begun (prārabdha), that which has been accumulated (saṃcita), and that which is yet to come (āgāmi)—as well as Māyā, are known as the objective forms of the delusion of the mind. || 59 ||
The partless (niṣkala) is a division of Śiva and is the cause of sound (nāda), the point (bindu), and so forth;
the specialized knowledge regarding their arousal is known as Mahāmāyā.

The Self (ātman) situated between Śiva and Śivā, that which is joined to the sides like a mirror, and that which is ripened by the nature of the object and the perceiver— this is known as concealment (tirobhāva). || 61 ||
Having thus explained the fifth impurity, now hear about the descent of power (śaktipāta):
one who is joined with both merit and demerit [is transformed] by the descent of Śiva’s power.
Their characteristic mark is discernment, and in liberation it is simply the state of being a person;
through their devotions toward Śiva’s devotees, they possess a state of mind that is free from aversion.
And faith in those seats is desired by the teacher of knowledge;
just as fire arises from a sun-gem merely through the proximity of the sun. (64)
By the mere presence of the guru, the disciple’s knowledge is illuminated;
it may become mild, very mild, intense, or even more intense. (65)
The wise man, having understood through their distinctions the fourfold varieties— namely the plantain, the ginger-wood, the fuel, and the root— as being both ripe and unripe. (66)
Knowledge, yoga, action, and conduct are the steps leading to the state that grants liberation;
these are called the Carya-pāda (the section on conduct) and the Kriyā-pāda (the section on ritual action). || 67 ||

"I am Śiva," and the yoga of contemplation, which leads to liberation through knowledge (sāyujya)—thus, in the Śaiva Āgama, this is the primary [teaching] regarding the sequence from the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati) away from the bonds (pāśa). (68)
In that regard, the instruction on mantras is said to have a threefold division;
it is traditionally known as the external state, the mental state, and the internal state. (69)
The trident, the mental state, and the mantra, as well as the instruction on internal existence— these constitute the noose, and Paśupati is the one who possesses them.

(235) Herein, yoga consists of the partless (niṣkala), the supportless (nirādhāra), and the support (ādhāra); it also comprises dissolution (laya), non-modification (avikāra), and enjoyment (bhoga), as well as the jewel (maṇi), the mantra, and the medicinal herb (auṣadha). || 71 ||
Thus, by this very meaning, one should demonstrate [it].
I shall fully proclaim its essence; listen with a one-pointed mind. (72)
The differentiation of the thirty-six principles is known as the knowledge of bonds (pāśajñāna);
and that which is proclaimed as transcending the principles is what constitutes the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna). (73)
The knowledge of both is indeed one and the same;
having thus understood this threefold [nature], union (sāyujya) becomes certain.
The state of the bound soul (paśu) is the noose of ignorance; it rests upon the knowledge of the Lord.
Indeed, the wise know the body to be composed of the seven constituents and to be impermanent. || 75 ||
The wise one should contemplate that the five elements, beginning with space, perish;
having transcended the other instrument (karaṇa), the knowledge of time and so forth perishes.
Beyond that is the triad of qualities (guṇatraya), then Śuddhavidyā, and Sadāśiva.
The vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is destroyed, and it becomes situated within the power of the *bindu*;
[it subdues] the body, the organs of knowledge, and the wind of the qualities (*guṇavāyu*).
In this way, one should demonstrate the five types of conceit and the five states;
one should meditate upon the principles (tattvas), beginning with Tattva and ending with Śakti, together with their respective entities.
The knowledge of reality consists of the state of the individual soul, while the eternal is the principle of Śiva;
thus, the thirty-six principles and whatever perception exists are brought to an end.
That knowledge and that vision of the self is called the knowledge of the Lord (*pati-jñāna*).
That knowledge which transcends the principles (*tattva*) is the knowledge of the Supreme Waking State (*parajāgrat*). (81)
The devouring of all is said to be that state which is like another's dream;
the knowledge of that, as well as the peace of the Vedas, is deep sleep, and that indeed is the supreme.
Then, having led [the disciple] to the self-luminous state of the Guru, which is the triad of ten, it is called the knowledge of the Lord; now hear concerning union (sāyujya) thereafter.
That state is the form of Śiva, and your state is the nature of the Self;
it is known as the word "asi," as union (sāyujya), and as the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). || 84 ||
They know that which is the supreme Vedānta to be the subtle Siddhānta;
the state of being of equal flavor (samarasī-bhāva) has been described, and now the state of being as a mother (mātṛ-bhāva) is spoken of.
Having abandoned all mental constructs, one should meditate on the thought "I am Śiva," completely free from all thoughts and devoid of even a single [conceptualization]. 86.
From the big toe to the crown of the head, that place is devoid of meditation;
it is both with form and formless, and free from the signified and the signifier.
Having realized that the light in the center is composed of Śiva, when it is manifested, there is no ear yet he hears, and there is no eye yet he sees. 88.
There is no sense of smell without a fragrant scent, nor is there speech without words; likewise, they know that there is no tongue that perceives taste, and no skin that perceives touch.

Thinking, "There is no hand," he does not grasp; thinking, "There are no feet," he does not walk; thinking, "There is no mind," [he perceives] the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving. (90)
Without the Mahāpuruṣa, the world does not exist; thus it is said that this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, always revolves and consumes [the fruits of action]. 91.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, it has acted with complete fullness;
it is the supreme, divine form of light, filled with the waters of dissolution.
It is secret, pure, supreme, blissful, immovable, and eternal; it is liberated from all principles, beyond reasoning, and inconceivable.
Place yourself within that, and place that within yourself;
having made it manifest as consisting of Śiva, one should not think of anything at all. 94.
One should abandon the knower, the knowledge, the teacher, the disciple, and indeed the object of knowledge;
one should instead attain that stainless reality which is the partless Śiva and consist of it. 95.

Thus, one should display the seal of silence (maunamudrā), which is the manifestation of dream-like reality. That meditation, that recitation, worship, and the performance of fire-offerings (homa)—this is the means of accomplishment (sādhana). (96)
The renunciant should contemplate all ritual acts as Śiva alone—[acts] which are the vessel for the sacred ford and which transcend the distinctions of caste and stage of life. || 97 ||

One should avoid [the recitation] regarding direction, place, location, and time, as well as the posture, whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, in the company of women, or even while eating. (98)
In the seasons of wind, cold, and heat; in fear, poverty, and passion; in pride, anger, and mental states; and in the delusion of knowledge and ignorance—[in all these, there is no change]. 99.
At all times and in every moment, remain unwavering in the state of Śiva;
there is nothing higher than the feet of the Guru, and no attainment greater than the realization of the Self. 100.

Therefore, the meaning of the word "Guru" is said to be the sequential process consisting of ten divisions, beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with the attainment of the Self (*ātmalābha*), which is the full emergence of the state of being (*pūrṇabhāva*). (101)

Through the instruction of the true guru, one who is liberated while living should reveal that supreme knowledge which is the form of the guru, and that supreme Śiva which is the form of the guru. (102)
The supreme light is the form of the Guru; that which is higher than the highest is the form of the Guru. O Guru, meditation is your embodiment; the state of devotion is your station.
The root of mantra is the word of the guru; the root of the form is the grace of the guru.
The guru is father, the guru is mother; they know everything to be composed of the guru. (104)
Therefore, one should behold the Guru as Śiva; union [with Him] becomes certain for one who knows the reality of the Sovereign Lord of Śivas and who shines with the nature of Śiva. 105.

They know the great-souled one who perceives the nine principles to be [the true teacher]; they know him who understands the meaning of the scriptures and the words of the guru in accordance with his own direct experience. (106)
Forgive this offense of mine committed through mind, speech, and body;
by its power, may there be the vision of the meaning of the glorious root, the feet of Śiva. 107.
The visible, the state of being visible, and the visible as the arising of the supreme—
thus ends the chapter on Knowledge and Vision in the *Candrajñāna*.
This is by Śiva Subrahmaṇya Śāstrin.
